Snipes died two days later after the hospital treating him said no blood was available for a needed transfusion. A coroner's jury acquitted Williamson on a self-defense claim, despite Snipes's own deathbed statement and his mother's witness testimony contradicting it. Fearing retaliation, the family buried him secretly at night in a grave whose location remains unknown to his surviving relatives, and much of the family fled the county. Snipes's killing, alongside the Moore's Ford lynchings that occurred in Georgia just one week later, prompted a young Morehouse College student, Martin Luther King Jr., to write a public letter condemning the state's racial violence. No one was ever held accountable.

name: James Earl Motley
summary: James Earl Motley, 27, died from head injuries in the Elmore County jail around 3:30 a.m. on November 20, 1966, hours after Deputy Harvey Conner stopped the car he was riding in for a traffic violation. When Motley told Conner he lacked jurisdiction because the stop had occurred in a different county, Conner ordered him out of the car; witnesses said Conner then struck Motley repeatedly in the head with a slapjack, and that state troopers who arrived as backup held Motley by the arms while he was beaten. Conner took the bleeding Motley to the county jail, where local authorities said he fell twice and struck his head before losing consciousness. An autopsy found multiple skull fractures and brain hemorrhage; a coroner concluded the fatal injury could have come from the beating, the falls, or some combination, and classified the death as “accidental.” A state grand jury declined to indict Conner on a homicide charge in January 1967. He was separately tried in federal court for violating Motley's civil rights; an all-white jury with one Black member returned a not-guilty verdict on April 12, 1967.

name: Thad Christian
summary: Thad Christian, 54, was fatally shot in the abdomen with a shotgun on August 30, 1965, while fishing with a friend at a creek in the rural community of Central City, west of Anniston. Robert Haynes, 41, had earlier told the two men to leave the area without saying whether he owned the property, then returned and shot Christian as they loaded their fishing gear into their car. Haynes was arrested and charged with murder, but pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of first-degree manslaughter and was sentenced to five years at a prison camp; how much of that sentence he actually served was not documented. Haynes died in a car accident three years later, in 1968. When the FBI reopened the case decades afterward, it found most surviving local records had been damaged by water and were illegible; one salvaged 1965 file noted a claim that several other Black men had also been at the creek that afternoon, a detail never further investigated.

name: Isaiah Henry
summary: Isaiah Henry, 38, a school bus driver and farmer who helped his Black neighbors prepare for voter registration tests, was found severely beaten on the side of a road in St. Helena Parish on July 28, 1954, one day after he voted in the Democratic primary. Unidentified men had called on him that morning and he left with them; he was later taken to a hospital in New Orleans. In early August 1954, sheriff's office deputies arrested a local police juror, Lester Hornsby, and a sheriff's deputy, Carl Womak, on charges of simple kidnapping and attempted murder; Womak had been the deputy assigned to the polling place where Henry voted. A contemporaneous news article quoted the assistant district attorney saying the two men were held because he believed they knew something about the beating, but no record indicates either man was ever indicted. Local jail logbooks, arrest warrants, and prosecutorial files from the case no longer exist. One of Henry's sons later said his father was likely beaten because of his political involvement.

name: John Earl Reese
summary: John Earl Reese, 16, was shot and killed on the night of October 22, 1955, while dancing with his cousins in a café in Mayflower, a small Black community near Longview. Perry Dean Ross, driving roughly 85 miles per hour, fired nine shots from a rifle into the café window as his car passed; Reese was killed, and two of his cousins were wounded. The same night, gunmen fired into at least one other home in the area where Black residents lived. The attacks were tied to local anger over a bond election to build a new school for Black children following the Brown v. Board of Education decision; Ross later admitted his anger over the new school had “a great deal” to do with the shooting. The local sheriff initially refused to investigate, insisting Black residents were responsible for their own community's shooting. Texas Rangers eventually interviewed over 300 people and identified Ross and a second man, Joe Simpson, both of whom confessed. Simpson's charges were dropped in exchange for his testimony against Ross, who was convicted of murder in April 1957 and given a two-to-five-year sentence that was immediately suspended; Simpson later pleaded guilty to the same charge and received an identical suspended sentence. Neither man served any time in prison.

name: Frank Andrews
summary: Frank Andrews, 27, was shot in the back and killed on November 28, 1964 outside Smith's Café in Lisman, Alabama, by Quinnie Donald, a white Choctaw County sheriff's chief deputy. Donald and another deputy said they were at the café, which served the local Black community, investigating illegal whiskey; Donald claimed Andrews advanced on a fellow deputy with a knife, a claim disputed by witness accounts. A local grand jury declined to indict, and no one was ever prosecuted for his death.

name: Alexis Patterson
summary: Alexis Patterson, 7, disappeared on the morning of May 3, 2002 after her stepfather walked her to a crosswalk roughly half a block from Hi-Mount Community School in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and a crossing guard escorted her across the street. She never arrived in her first-grade classroom; classmates later reported seeing her crying on the playground before and after the school day. Her disappearance prompted one of the largest search efforts in Milwaukee police history, but no arrests have ever been made and Alexis has never been found.

name: Nacomie Freeman
summary: Nacomie Freeman, 24, was shot in the stomach and pushed out of a moving truck in the 1600 block of West Denton Avenue in Phoenix, Arizona, on June 24, 2004. Witnesses reported seeing her pushed from a dark-colored, late-1990s-model short-bed truck; she was pronounced dead at the scene. The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office has said investigators developed some leads but have never made an arrest.

name: Quincy Booker
summary: Quincy Booker, 36, was shot and killed in a drive-by shooting near the intersection of Arno Avenue and Santa Fe Avenue Southeast in Albuquerque, New Mexico, on July 17, 2011. Witnesses said four men got out of a blue Dodge Neon and opened fire, hitting him more than a dozen times, next to a church filled with people on a Sunday. The attackers fled immediately, and the case has remained unsolved since.

name: Julius Dubouse
summary: Julius Dubouse, 45, died in Anchorage, Alaska in the early morning hours of December 3, 1998, after an accelerant was thrown through the back window of his residence. The Anchorage Police Department's Cold Case Section, whose mission is to systematically review unsolved deaths in its jurisdiction, lists his death among its open homicide investigations. No arrest has ever been made.

name: Kierre Davies
summary: Kierre Davies, 27, was shot and killed alongside his friend and fellow rapper, 28-year-old Jaquan Gatewood, in the early morning hours of November 19, 2022, outside a house near the North Dakota State University campus in Fargo. Both men were at a gathering at the home; neither lived there. Police say everyone involved knew each other and have said there is no danger to the public, but more than a year later no arrest has been made and the case remains open.

name: Emmett Till
summary: Emmett Till, 14, of Chicago, was abducted from his great-uncle's home near Money, Mississippi, on August 28, 1955, and beaten, shot, and thrown into the Tallahatchie River after Carolyn Bryant, a white woman working at a local store, accused him of grabbing her and making sexual advances. Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam, her husband and brother-in-law, were tried for murder and acquitted by an all-white jury within about an hour; months later, protected by double jeopardy, they confessed to the killing in a paid magazine interview. Neither man was ever punished, and no one has ever been convicted in the case. Till's mother's decision to hold an open-casket funeral, and photographs of his mutilated body published in Jet magazine, helped galvanize the civil rights movement.

name: Malcolm X
summary: Malcolm X, 39, was shot and killed while delivering a speech at the Audubon Ballroom in the Washington Heights neighborhood of Manhattan on February 21, 1965. Talmadge Hayer (also known as Mujahid Abdul Halim) was caught at the scene and confessed to being one of the shooters; he, along with Muhammad Aziz and Khalil Islam, were convicted of murder in 1966. Aziz and Islam always maintained their innocence, and in November 2021 a joint reinvestigation by the Manhattan District Attorney's office and the men's attorneys resulted in both convictions being vacated, citing withheld exculpatory evidence. Hayer had named four other men as participants in a 1978 affidavit, but that information was never used to reopen the case at the time, and no one beyond Hayer has ever been properly convicted of the killing.

name: Fred Hampton
summary: Fred Hampton, 21, chairman of the Illinois chapter of the Black Panther Party, was shot and killed in his bed during a pre-dawn raid on his Chicago apartment on December 4, 1969, carried out by a tactical unit assembled by Cook County State's Attorney Edward Hanrahan in coordination with the FBI. Fellow Panther Mark Clark was also killed. A coroner's inquest initially ruled the deaths justifiable homicide, but a 13-year civil lawsuit brought by survivors and the victims' families produced evidence of FBI involvement, including an informant who supplied a floor plan of the apartment marking Hampton's bed. The case ended in a 1982 settlement, not a criminal conviction: no officer, agent, or official involved in the raid was ever criminally charged or convicted for the deaths.

name: Amadou Diallo
summary: Amadou Diallo, 23, an unarmed immigrant from Guinea, was shot and killed just after midnight on February 4, 1999 outside his Bronx apartment building by four plainclothes NYPD Street Crime Unit officers, who fired 41 rounds, 19 of which struck him. The officers said they believed Diallo, who was reaching for his wallet, matched the description of a rape suspect and that they mistook the wallet for a gun. A Bronx grand jury indicted all four officers on second-degree murder and other charges; the trial was moved to Albany, and on February 25, 2000, the jury acquitted all four of every charge. The Department of Justice later found insufficient evidence to bring federal charges. No one has ever been held criminally responsible for Diallo's death.

name: Sean Bell
summary: Sean Bell, 23, was shot and killed by NYPD undercover officers in Jamaica, Queens in the early morning hours of November 25, 2006 — the day he was to be married. Officers fired 50 rounds at Bell and his two friends, Trent Benefield and Joseph Guzman, as the men left Bell's bachelor party; no weapon was ever recovered from the vehicle. Detectives Gescard Isnora and Michael Oliver were charged with manslaughter and Detective Marc Cooper with reckless endangerment. In April 2008, a judge acquitted all three of every charge, ruling that prosecutors had not proven their actions were unjustified. Federal prosecutors declined to bring civil rights charges. No one has ever been held criminally responsible for Bell's death.

name: Trayvon Martin
summary: Trayvon Martin, 17, was shot and killed by George Zimmerman, a neighborhood watch volunteer, inside a gated community in Sanford, Florida on February 26, 2012. Martin was unarmed, walking back from a convenience store. Zimmerman, who had called police to report Martin as suspicious before following him, claimed he acted in self-defense during a physical altercation. Unlike most cases in this archive, this one did reach trial: charges were filed after weeks of public pressure, and a jury acquitted Zimmerman of second-degree murder and manslaughter in July 2013. The county medical examiner's report is unambiguous on the underlying facts — Martin died of a gunshot wound to the chest, and the manner of death is listed as homicide. This case is classified here as Unresolved — No Conviction, not Unsolved: the distinction matters, since a full trial did take place and its outcome is a matter of public record, unlike the majority of cases in this archive where no charges were ever filed at all. The U.S. Department of Justice separately investigated and did not bring federal civil rights charges. No one has ever been held criminally responsible for Martin's death.

name: Freddie Gray
summary: Freddie Gray, 25, suffered a fatal spinal cord injury while in the back of a Baltimore Police transport van after his arrest on April 12, 2015, and died a week later. The city medical examiner ruled his death a homicide. Six officers were criminally charged, with counts ranging from misconduct in office to second-degree “depraved heart” murder. Four officers went to trial: three were acquitted by a judge and one trial ended in a hung jury. Prosecutors then dropped all remaining charges against the other officers in July 2016, securing no convictions. The U.S. Department of Justice separately reviewed the case and declined federal prosecution. No one has ever been convicted in Freddie Gray's death.

name: Breonna Taylor
summary: Breonna Taylor, 26, an emergency room technician, was shot and killed by Louisville Metro Police officers executing a no-knock search warrant at her apartment shortly after midnight on March 13, 2020. The warrant was later found to have been based on falsified information. Taylor's boyfriend, believing intruders had broken in, fired a shot that struck an officer; police returned more than 30 rounds, killing Taylor. A local grand jury declined to charge any officer for her death. The U.S. Department of Justice later brought federal civil rights charges against four current and former officers; only one, Brett Hankison, was convicted, for firing blindly into the apartment — not for killing Taylor, since his shots never struck her. No one has ever been charged with, or convicted of, causing Taylor's death itself.

name: Rekia Boyd
summary: Rekia Boyd, 22, was shot and killed by off-duty Chicago Police Detective Dante Servin near Douglas Park on the city's West Side in the early hours of March 21, 2012. Servin, in his car in a nearby alley, fired five shots over his shoulder at a group Boyd was part of, striking a man in the hand and Boyd in the back of the head; he said he believed one of the group had pulled a gun, but no weapon was ever found. Servin was charged nearly two years later with involuntary manslaughter and reckless discharge of a firearm. At his 2015 bench trial, the judge issued a directed verdict of not guilty before the defense even presented its case, ruling that Servin's conduct was intentional rather than reckless — meaning prosecutors had charged the wrong offense — while noting Servin's actions were “beyond reckless.” Because of double jeopardy, he could never be retried on a more serious charge. No one has ever been convicted in Boyd's death.

name: Eric Garner
summary: Eric Garner, 43, died on July 17, 2014 after NYPD Officer Daniel Pantaleo placed him in an apparent chokehold — a maneuver banned under NYPD policy — while arresting him on suspicion of selling untaxed loose cigarettes on a Staten Island street corner. Bystander video captured Garner repeating “I can't breathe” eleven times before he lost consciousness. The city medical examiner ruled his death a homicide, citing the chokehold as a contributing cause. A Staten Island grand jury declined to indict Pantaleo in December 2014. The Department of Justice's five-year federal civil rights investigation ended in July 2019, one day before the fifth anniversary of Garner's death, with Attorney General William Barr declining to bring charges. Pantaleo was fired from the NYPD in an internal disciplinary proceeding later that year, but no criminal charge was ever filed against him or anyone else involved in Garner's death.

name: Tamir Rice
summary: Tamir Rice, 12, was shot and killed by rookie Cleveland Police Officer Timothy Loehmann on November 22, 2014, within two seconds of Loehmann's patrol car skidding to a stop beside him outside a recreation center. Rice had been playing with a pellet gun; the 911 caller told the dispatcher the gun was “probably fake” and the person waving it was “probably a juvenile,” but that information was never relayed to the responding officers. A grand jury declined to indict Loehmann or his partner, Frank Garmback, in December 2015, with the county prosecutor calling the shooting a “perfect storm of human error” rather than a crime. The Department of Justice closed a five-year federal civil rights investigation in December 2020 without charges. No one has ever been criminally charged in Tamir Rice's death.

name: Philando Castile
summary: Philando Castile, 32, a St. Paul-area elementary school cafeteria supervisor, was shot and killed by St. Anthony Police Officer Jeronimo Yanez during a traffic stop in Falcon Heights, Minnesota on July 6, 2016. Castile, who had a permit to carry, calmly informed Yanez he had a firearm in the car; Yanez fired seven shots, striking him five times, as Castile's girlfriend Diamond Reynolds and her 4-year-old daughter sat in the car. Reynolds began livestreaming the aftermath on Facebook within moments, and the video was viewed by millions. Yanez was charged with second-degree manslaughter and two counts of endangering Reynolds and her daughter; a jury acquitted him of all charges on June 16, 2017, after roughly 27 hours of deliberation. No one has ever been convicted in Castile's death.

name: Stephon Clark
summary: Stephon Clark, 22, was shot and killed by Sacramento Police officers Terrence Mercadal and Jared Robinet in his grandmother's backyard on March 18, 2018, after they responded to a report of vandalism and pursued him on foot. The officers said they believed Clark was pointing a gun at them in the dark; he was holding only a cellphone. Sacramento County District Attorney Anne Marie Schubert announced in March 2019 that no criminal charges would be filed. Days later, California Attorney General Xavier Becerra's independent state review reached the same conclusion. In September 2019, federal prosecutors also declined to bring civil rights charges. Three separate reviews — county, state, and federal — each concluded independently that no charges could be sustained, and no one has ever been convicted in Clark's death.

name: Michael Brown
summary: Michael Brown, 18, was shot and killed by Ferguson, Missouri Police Officer Darren Wilson on August 9, 2014, following a confrontation after Wilson stopped Brown and a friend for walking in the street. Brown's body remained in the street for roughly four hours afterward, which inflamed already-tense relations between the majority-Black city and its overwhelmingly white police force. A St. Louis County grand jury declined to indict Wilson in November 2014. The Department of Justice separately cleared Wilson of civil rights violations in March 2015, while issuing a scathing report finding Ferguson's police and courts had systematically targeted Black residents for revenue rather than public safety. In 2020, the county's first Black prosecutor, Wesley Bell, reopened the case at the family's request and, after a five-month independent review, announced in 2020 that he too could not prove murder or manslaughter charges. Three separate reviewing authorities have now each declined to charge Wilson, who resigned days after the grand jury decision; no one has ever been charged in Brown's death.

name: Alton Sterling
summary: Alton Sterling, 37, a father of five who sold homemade CDs outside a Baton Rouge convenience store, was shot and killed by Officers Blane Salamoni and Howie Lake II on July 5, 2016, during a struggle after the two officers responded to a report of a man threatening someone with a gun. Cellphone video of the roughly 90-second encounter, showing Sterling pinned to the ground when he was shot, circulated widely and prompted nationwide protests. The Department of Justice declined to bring federal civil rights charges in May 2017. Nearly a year later, in March 2018, Louisiana's attorney general separately declined to bring state charges, calling the shooting “justifiable” and citing a toxicology report showing Sterling had drugs in his system. No one has ever been criminally charged in Sterling's death.

name: John Crawford III
summary: John Crawford III, 22, was shot and killed by Beavercreek, Ohio Police Officer Sean Williams inside a Walmart store on August 5, 2014, while talking on his cell phone and holding an unboxed BB/pellet air rifle he had picked up from a store shelf. A 911 caller, Ronald Ritchie, had told dispatchers a man was waving a gun at customers — an account store surveillance video later contradicted, showing Crawford never pointed the item at anyone. A special Greene County grand jury declined to indict Williams in September 2014, the same day the Department of Justice opened its own civil rights investigation; that federal review closed in July 2017 without charges, finding insufficient evidence that Williams had willfully violated Crawford's civil rights. No one has ever been charged in Crawford's death.

name: Sandra Bland
summary: Sandra Bland, 28, was found dead in her cell at the Waller County Jail in Hempstead, Texas on July 13, 2015, three days after Texas State Trooper Brian Encinia arrested her during a traffic stop in nearby Prairie View for failing to signal a lane change. Dashcam video showed the stop escalating after Bland questioned why she had to put out her cigarette, ending with Encinia drawing a Taser and pulling her from her car. Her death was ruled a suicide by asphyxiation. A Waller County grand jury found no criminal wrongdoing by jailers or the sheriff's office, but did indict Encinia on a misdemeanor perjury charge for falsely writing that he removed Bland from her car to conduct a “safer traffic investigation.” That charge — the only criminal charge ever filed against anyone in connection with Bland's death — was dropped in June 2017 after Encinia agreed to surrender his peace officer license and never work in law enforcement again. No one has ever been convicted of any crime related to Bland's arrest, treatment, or death.

name: Terence Crutcher
summary: Terence Crutcher, 40, was shot and killed by Tulsa Police Officer Betty Shelby on September 16, 2016, after she encountered him beside his stalled SUV in the middle of a north Tulsa street. Video from a police helicopter piloted by Shelby's own husband and from officers' body cameras showed Crutcher walking toward his vehicle with his hands visible before Shelby fired; the helicopter pilot could be heard remarking that Crutcher “looks like a bad dude.” Shelby testified she believed Crutcher was reaching into the vehicle for a weapon; no weapon was found. She was charged with first-degree manslaughter and, after nine hours of jury deliberation, acquitted of all charges on May 17, 2017. Crutcher's family called the verdict an injustice; no one has ever been convicted in his death.

name: Samuel DuBose
summary: Samuel DuBose, 43, was shot in the head and killed by University of Cincinnati Police Officer Ray Tensing during a traffic stop on July 19, 2015, after Tensing pulled him over for a missing front license plate. Body camera video showed a brief exchange over DuBose's license before he began to drive away; Tensing testified he was dragged by the car and feared for his life, while the county prosecutor called the shooting “asinine” and “totally unwarranted” when announcing a murder indictment less than two weeks later. Two separate juries, in trials roughly eight months apart, deadlocked and produced mistrials in 2016 and 2017. Hamilton County's prosecutor then dropped the case rather than pursue a third trial, saying jurors had told him he would never get twelve people to agree to convict a police officer. No one has ever been convicted in DuBose's death.

name: Keith Lamont Scott
summary: Keith Lamont Scott, 43, a father of seven, was shot and killed by Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Officer Brentley Vinson on September 20, 2016, in an apartment complex parking lot. Officers were at the complex to serve a warrant on someone else when they encountered Scott, who has a brain injury, sitting in his SUV; police said body-camera video showed a gun in his hand as he exited the vehicle after repeated orders to drop it, while Scott's wife, who recorded the aftermath on her phone, said he had no gun and was unarmed. A firearm was recovered at the scene with Scott's fingerprints and DNA. After a two-month investigation, Mecklenburg County District Attorney Andrew Murray announced in November 2016 that Vinson — who is also Black — had acted lawfully, a conclusion 15 prosecutors in his office reached unanimously. No charges were ever filed against Vinson or any other officer at the scene.

name: Ezell Ford
summary: Ezell Ford, 25, who his family said had a serious mental illness, was shot and killed by LAPD Officers Sharlton Wampler and Antonio Villegas on August 11, 2014, during a struggle after the officers stopped him while he was walking near his South Los Angeles home. Police said Ford grabbed for Wampler's holstered weapon during the struggle; DNA evidence supported that he was on top of Wampler at the time of the shooting. The Los Angeles Police Commission ruled in June 2015 that Wampler had no legal justification to stop Ford in the first place, making the entire encounter — and by extension the shooting — out of department policy. Despite that finding, the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office announced in January 2017, more than two years after the shooting, that neither officer would face criminal charges, concluding both had acted in lawful self-defense. No officer in Los Angeles County had been criminally charged for an on-duty shooting since 2000, and none was in Ford's case either.

name: Danroy Henry Jr.
summary: Danroy “DJ” Henry Jr., 20, a Pace University football player, was shot and killed by Pleasantville, New York Police Officer Aaron Hess on October 17, 2010, in a shopping center parking lot after officers responded to a bar disturbance following Pace's homecoming game. Henry was driving away in his car when Hess, on foot, ended up on the hood of the vehicle and fired through the windshield, saying he feared for his life; Henry's family disputed that account, saying Hess ran into the car's path. A Westchester County grand jury found no reasonable cause for an indictment in March 2011. The U.S. Department of Justice separately investigated and announced in 2015 that it would bring no federal civil rights charges. In 2023, more than a decade later, Westchester's District Attorney's office reopened the case as part of an independent review and again concluded there was no legal basis to prosecute. No one has ever been charged in Henry's death.

name: Kenneth Chamberlain Sr.
summary: Kenneth Chamberlain Sr., 68, a retired Marine and 20-year Westchester County corrections officer with a chronic heart condition, was shot and killed in his own White Plains apartment on November 19, 2011, after his medical alert pendant was triggered accidentally. Chamberlain repeatedly told police through the door that he did not need help and asked them to leave; after roughly an hour, officers broke the door down, used a Taser and beanbag rounds, and then fatally shot him. A Westchester County grand jury declined to indict any officer in May 2012. The Department of Justice's Southern District of New York investigated separately and closed its inquiry in 2017 without federal charges, and a federal civil jury cleared the city and the officer of liability in 2016. No one has ever been criminally charged in Chamberlain's death.

name: Jonathan Ferrell
summary: Jonathan Ferrell, 24, a former Florida A&M football player, was shot and killed by Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Officer Randall “Wes” Kerrick on September 14, 2013, after crawling from a wrecked car and banging on a nearby house's door seeking help; the resident, mistaking him for a home invader, called 911. Kerrick fired 12 rounds, striking Ferrell 10 times, eight while he was already on the ground; the two other responding officers did not fire. Kerrick was charged with voluntary manslaughter — the first Charlotte officer ever charged for an on-duty shooting — but a 2015 jury deadlocked 8-4 in favor of acquittal after four days of deliberation, resulting in a mistrial. North Carolina's attorney general declined to seek a retrial, and the charge was formally dismissed. No one has ever been convicted in Ferrell's death.

name: Milton Hall
summary: Milton Hall, 49, a homeless man with a documented history of mental illness, was shot and killed by six Saginaw, Michigan police officers on July 1, 2012, in a parking lot after a dispute with a convenience store clerk. Eight officers formed a semicircle around Hall, who held a small pocketknife; after a police dog was allowed to bark and snap at him, six officers opened fire, striking him 11 times out of 46 rounds fired, continuing to shoot after he had collapsed. The Saginaw County prosecutor and the Michigan Attorney General's office both declined to bring criminal charges, finding the officers had not acted with criminal intent. The Department of Justice opened its own civil rights investigation and announced in February 2014 that it too would not prosecute, citing insufficient evidence of willful misconduct. No one has ever been charged in Hall's death.

name: Miriam Carey
summary: Miriam Carey, 34, a dental hygienist from Stamford, Connecticut, was shot and killed by U.S. Secret Service and Capitol Police officers on October 3, 2013, after a seven-minute car chase that began when she drove into a restricted checkpoint near the White House with her 1-year-old daughter in the car and ended near the U.S. Capitol. Carey, who her family said had been hospitalized for postpartum depression, was unarmed; two officers each fired nine rounds in the final confrontation, striking her five times. Her daughter was found unharmed in the car. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia announced in July 2014 that it found insufficient evidence to bring federal civil rights or local charges against any officer involved. No one has ever been charged in Carey's death.

name: Daniel Prude
summary: Daniel Prude, 41, a father of five visiting Rochester, New York from Chicago, died on March 30, 2020, a week after Rochester police officers restrained him naked on a snow-covered street during a mental health crisis. Body-camera video, not made public until September 2020, showed officers placing a mesh “spit hood” over his head and pressing his face into the pavement for roughly two minutes until he stopped breathing. The Monroe County medical examiner ruled his death a homicide from “complications of asphyxia in the setting of physical restraint.” New York Attorney General Letitia James's office presented the case to a grand jury, which voted 15–5 in February 2021 not to indict any of the three officers involved. No one has ever been charged in Prude's death.

name: Manuel Ellis
summary: Manuel “Manny” Ellis, 33, died in a south Tacoma, Washington intersection on March 3, 2020, after Tacoma police officers tackled, punched, shocked him with a Taser, and restrained him face-down while he repeatedly told them he could not breathe. The Pierce County medical examiner ruled his death a homicide caused by oxygen deprivation from physical restraint. Washington's attorney general charged three officers in 2021 — the first time the state's AG had criminally charged officers for unlawful use of deadly force, using a new voter-approved police accountability law. After a nine-week trial, a Pierce County jury acquitted all three officers of every charge on December 21, 2023. The officers each subsequently received $500,000 to voluntarily leave the department. No one has ever been convicted in Ellis's death.

name: Relisha Rudd
summary: Relisha Rudd, 8, disappeared from Washington, D.C.'s D.C. General Family Shelter, where she lived with her mother and siblings, in early 2014. She was last seen on security footage on March 1, 2014, at a Northeast D.C. hotel with Kahlil Tatum, a 51-year-old shelter janitor with a prior felony record whom her mother had allowed to take her overnight. Her absence from school went unreported for roughly 18 days until a school counselor raised the alarm. Tatum was later found to have shot and killed his wife before being found dead of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound on April 1, 2014. Investigators believe Tatum killed Relisha before taking his own life, though her body has never been found and no charges have ever been filed in connection with her disappearance. Her case remains open more than a decade later.

name: Asha Degree
summary: Asha Degree, 9, disappeared from her family's home in Shelby, North Carolina in the early morning hours of February 14, 2000. Several motorists reported seeing her walking alone south along Highway 18 around 3:30–4:00 a.m. in heavy rain, carrying a backpack she had packed herself; when one driver slowed to approach her, she ran into the woods. Her parents discovered her missing later that morning. Eighteen months later, her backpack was found buried along the same highway, about 26 miles from her home. In 2024, investigators searched multiple properties belonging to a local family, seizing a vehicle matching a description linked to the night she disappeared, and increased the reward to $100,000; a person reportedly told police in 2024 that a member of that family had once said “I killed Asha Degree.” No arrest has ever been made, and Asha has never been found.

name: Keeshae Jacobs
summary: Keeshae Jacobs, 21, disappeared in Richmond, Virginia after visiting a male friend's home on September 26, 2016. She texted her mother, Toni Jacobs, that she had arrived safely and would see her the next day; she was never heard from again. Richmond Police publicly stated in November 2017 that they believed foul play was involved, and in 2023 named a man, Otis Tucker, as a suspect in her disappearance; Tucker had given Jacobs's mother conflicting accounts of when he last saw her. In November 2022, Tucker was separately arrested and charged with second-degree murder and evidence tampering in the death of a different woman in Florida. He has never been charged in connection with Jacobs's disappearance. No arrest has been made and Keeshae has never been found.

name: Kierra Coles
summary: Kierra Coles, 26, a U.S. Postal Service letter carrier who was three months pregnant, disappeared from Chicago's Chatham neighborhood on October 2, 2018, after calling in sick to work. Surveillance footage that day showed her walking near her apartment in her postal uniform despite having called out; her car was later found parked on her block with her phone, purse, and lunch bag still inside. Chicago Police announced within two weeks that they suspected foul play. In 2022, police released additional surveillance video showing Coles withdrawing cash at a Walgreens ATM and driving off with a man identified as a person of interest shortly before her disappearance; that man was questioned but gave varying accounts and has never been arrested. The U.S. Postal Inspection Service raised its reward to $250,000 in 2026, the largest the agency offers. No arrest has ever been made and Coles has never been found.

name: Nakyla Williams
summary: Nakyla Williams, 24, a hairstylist who ran a salon out of her basement, disappeared in Indianapolis, Indiana on November 8, 2021, after a doorbell camera captured her getting into a loud, gray or white pickup truck outside her mother's home. She was later seen at a different residence that evening before leaving and never being heard from again. Her family identified a man named Bestin (or Destyn) Hoyle as the last person known to be with her; police sought him for questioning, though they have not classified him as a formal suspect. Her mother has said Hoyle left the state for Flint, Michigan shortly after Williams disappeared and deleted his social media interactions with her. Her family believes she may have been trafficked. No arrest has ever been made and Williams has never been found.

name: Jahi Turner
summary: Jahi Turner, 2, disappeared from a Golden Hill-area playground in San Diego on April 25, 2002, while in the care of his stepfather, Tieray Jones, whose 18-year-old Navy sailor wife was deployed at sea. Jones told police he left Jahi with a woman and other children at the park to buy a soda and returned to find them all gone; police found inconsistencies in his account but lacked evidence to charge him at the time. The case went cold for 14 years until new evidence, including a journal entry Jones wrote to his wife describing Jahi as unresponsive after a fall two days before he was reported missing, led to a murder charge in 2016. A 2018 jury deadlocked 10–2 in favor of acquittal on second-degree murder, and 10–2 in favor of conviction on the lesser charge of involuntary manslaughter; the judge declared a mistrial and later denied prosecutors' request for a second trial, finding it unlikely any future jury could reach a unanimous verdict given the missing body and 16-year delay. No one has ever been convicted, and Jahi has never been found.

name: Anwar Green
summary: Anwar Green disappeared in Newark, New Jersey on January 19, 2001, after he and his friend Rahim Martin cashed a civil lawsuit settlement check for over $8,000 at a bank in downtown Newark. Surveillance footage showed Green appearing nervous and repeatedly glancing at the door inside the bank. The two men were last seen together at a nearby office building, where Martin briefly called his uncle from a lobby payphone without going up to see him. The day after the pair were reported missing, a man's burned and murdered body was found inside a deliberately set house fire in Newark; that body was identified as Martin in August 2010, nine years later, using DNA technology unavailable at the time of his death. No trace of Green has ever been found, and investigators believe both men were the victims of a robbery connected to the cash they were carrying.

name: Carolyn, Sheketah, Barry & Brandon Brown
summary: Carolyn Denise Brown, 27, and her three children — 10-year-old Sheketah, 6-year-old Barry, and 2-year-old Brandon — disappeared from their Port St. Lucie, Florida home in July 1985. Carolyn's mother alerted police in August after weeks without contact; officers found the home undisturbed at first glance, but Carolyn's purse held identification cut into pieces, an untouched meal sat on the dining table, and a freshly repainted wall concealed bloodstains beneath. Carolyn's husband and the children's father, James Michael Brown, later confessed in detail to killing all four, telling investigators where he said he disposed of each body — locations that were searched without any remains ever being recovered. Court-appointed psychiatrists diagnosed James as a paranoid schizophrenic experiencing hallucinations; a jury found him not guilty by reason of insanity in the deaths of Carolyn and Sheketah, and he was never separately charged for Barry and Brandon's deaths because their locations couldn't be confirmed. He was committed to a Florida mental health facility, later released to a halfway house, and was free by 1997. No family member has ever been found, and no one has ever been convicted of a crime in their deaths.

name: Jalesa Chantell Reynolds
summary: Jalesa Chantell Reynolds, a shy teenager described by loved ones as more outgoing online than in person, disappeared from Scotland Neck, North Carolina on February 22, 2010. She had logged onto Facebook that morning from the public library, then logged on again that afternoon from the home of Dwayne Hosea Davis, a registered sex offender with a prior rape conviction. Authorities believe she left Davis's residence sometime between 2:00 and 3:00 p.m. that day; she has never been heard from since. No arrest has ever been made and Jalesa has never been found.

name: Tasha Shante Wright
summary: Tasha Shante Wright, 10, a gifted-and-talented fourth-grader, disappeared while walking a short distance within her own apartment complex in east Dallas, Texas on October 14, 1989. She successfully delivered a message from her mother to a neighbor's apartment, but never made it back to her own unit only a few doors away. An unconfirmed witness sighting placed her in a nearby breezeway shortly afterward, and she may have been seen staring at nearby bushes moments before vanishing. Extensive searches by police, search dogs, and helicopters covering a five-mile radius found no trace of her. No suspect has ever been publicly named and Tasha has never been found.

name: Barbara Jean Dreher
summary: Barbara Jean Dreher, 39, a mother of five who had worked as a Washington, D.C. public school secretary for fifteen years, disappeared on August 12, 1984 after dropping her two young sons off at her adult daughter's home, telling them she was going to pick up some money and would return shortly. Days later, her son spotted her burgundy Oldsmobile being driven by an unfamiliar man; he followed the car, called police, and identified the driver at the scene. Because the car had not been reported stolen, the man was released without arrest, though a ski mask, gloves, and rope were found inside the impounded vehicle. In 2018, D.C. police's cold case squad examined whether skeletal remains found in a Southeast D.C. apartment crawl space could be Dreher's, using DNA comparison; no match has been publicly confirmed. No one has ever been charged, and Barbara has never been found.

name: Dannette & Jeannette Millbrook
summary: Dannette and Jeannette Millbrook, 15-year-old fraternal twins, disappeared in Augusta, Georgia on March 18, 1990, after walking to a nearby gas station for snacks and telling their mother a man in a van had followed part of their route earlier that day. A gas station clerk was the last person to see them; nothing further is known about the man in the van. The Richmond County Sheriff's Office concluded the girls were runaways based on hearsay and closed the case in 1991, despite their mother's insistence they would not have left voluntarily. The case sat effectively unworked for over two decades until a newly elected sheriff reopened it in 2013; investigators have since interviewed witnesses, canvassed the area, and collected DNA samples from family members, but the case remains unsolved. Their case is believed to be one of the only unresolved disappearances of twins in American history.

name: Pshara Marie Jones
summary: Pshara Marie Jones, 20, a pharmacy employee, left her family's home in Claremore, Oklahoma on foot and without her phone on the evening of September 21, 2015, following an argument. Bank records show two transactions that same night, including one at a convenience store, but no account activity since. She never returned for medication she took for a mental health condition and never showed up for her next shift at the pharmacy where she worked. Her mother did not report her missing for roughly two weeks, initially expecting her to return or call as she reportedly had after past arguments. The Claremore Police Department's chief investigator has stated publicly that investigators strongly believe foul play was involved. No arrest has ever been made and Pshara has never been found.

name: The Clinton Avenue Five
summary: Melvin Pittman, 17, Ernest Taylor, 17, Alvin Turner, 16, Randy Johnson, 16, and Michael McDowell, 16 — five teenagers known as the Clinton Avenue Five — vanished together in Newark, New Jersey on August 20, 1978, after playing basketball and getting into a pickup truck driven by Lee Anthony Evans, a local handyman who paid them in odd jobs. The case went cold as a missing-persons file for three decades until 2008, when Evans's cousin Philander Hampton, in police custody on an unrelated charge, confessed after a 13-hour interrogation that Evans had lured the boys to a vacant house, locked them in a closet at gunpoint over a stolen-marijuana dispute, and set the building on fire, killing all five. Hampton pleaded guilty and received a 10-year sentence plus $15,000 in relocation money in exchange for testifying against Evans. At Evans's 2011 trial, where he represented himself, a jury acquitted him of all ten murder-related charges, finding the prosecution's case — built almost entirely on Hampton's confession, with no bodies or physical evidence ever recovered — insufficient. No one has ever been convicted of killing the five boys, whose remains have never been found.

name: Anthony Lamar Smith
summary: Anthony Lamar Smith, 24, was shot and killed by St. Louis Police Officer Jason Stockley on December 20, 2011, after a high-speed chase that began when Stockley believed he witnessed a drug transaction outside a Church's Chicken. Dashcam audio captured Stockley telling his partner “we're killing this [expletive], don't you know it” less than a minute before shooting Smith five times. Prosecutors alleged Stockley then planted a revolver in Smith's car — only Stockley's DNA was found on the gun, not Smith's. Stockley was charged with first-degree murder in 2016 and chose to have his case decided by a judge rather than a jury; in September 2017, Circuit Judge Timothy Wilson acquitted him, writing the state had not proven its case beyond a reasonable doubt and remarking that “an urban heroin dealer not in possession of a firearm would be an anomaly.” No one has ever been convicted in Smith's death.

name: Christian Taylor
summary: Christian Taylor, 19, an Angelo State University football player, was shot and killed by rookie Arlington, Texas Police Officer Brad Miller on August 7, 2015, inside a car dealership showroom he had broken into and was vandalizing while, an autopsy later showed, under the influence of a hallucinogen. Miller broke from his training officer and entered the showroom alone without informing his supervisor, then shot Taylor, who was unarmed, four times as Taylor advanced toward him after refusing to get on the ground. Miller was fired days later for what the police chief called a “catastrophic” tactical decision to confront Taylor alone. A Tarrant County grand jury declined to indict Miller in June 2016. No one has ever been charged in Taylor's death.

name: Kajieme Powell
summary: Kajieme Powell, 25, was shot and killed by St. Louis Police Officers Nicholas Shelton and Ellis Brown outside a convenience store on August 19, 2014 — ten days after the shooting of Michael Brown in nearby Ferguson. Officers responding to a report of shoplifting and a man carrying a knife found Powell, who witnesses said was in mental distress; a bystander's cellphone video showed police firing 12 shots roughly 23 seconds after arriving on scene, as Powell advanced holding what a later analysis confirmed was a knife. St. Louis Circuit Attorney Jennifer Joyce reviewed forensic evidence, witness accounts, and a 3-D spatial reconstruction before announcing in November 2015 that no charges would be filed, concluding a criminal violation could not be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. A use-of-force expert later hired by Powell's family disputed the analysis Joyce's office relied on. No one has ever been charged in Powell's death.

name: VonDerrit Myers Jr.
summary: VonDerrit Myers Jr., 18, was shot and killed by an off-duty St. Louis police officer, Jason Flanery, working a private security patrol job on October 8, 2014, in the city's Shaw neighborhood — exactly two months after Michael Brown's death in nearby Ferguson. Police said Myers ran from the officer, then turned and fired three shots at him during a foot chase before Flanery returned fire, striking Myers multiple times; a stolen 9mm handgun was recovered at the scene. Myers's family disputed that he was armed at the moment he was shot and said the investigation contained inconsistencies. St. Louis Circuit Attorney Jennifer Joyce reviewed the case independently of a grand jury and announced in May 2015 that criminal charges could not be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. No one has ever been charged in Myers's death.

name: Quintonio LeGrier & Bettie Jones
summary: Quintonio LeGrier, 19, a Northern Illinois University student experiencing a mental health crisis, and Bettie Jones, 55, his family's downstairs neighbor, were both shot and killed by Chicago Police Officer Robert Rialmo on December 26, 2015, while responding to a domestic disturbance call. Jones opened her door to direct officers upstairs; LeGrier came down the stairs swinging an aluminum bat, and Rialmo fired eight shots, six striking LeGrier and one accidentally striking Jones, whom police immediately acknowledged was an innocent bystander. The Cook County State's Attorney's Office declined to bring criminal charges in 2017, finding insufficient evidence to disprove self-defense. The city's own police oversight agency later found Rialmo's account “inconsistent and ultimately unreliable” and recommended his firing; the Chicago Police Board unanimously fired him in 2019, though only over the Jones shooting — a separate civil jury found the LeGrier shooting itself justified. No one has ever been criminally charged in either death.

name: Willie McCoy
summary: Willie McCoy, 20, a local rapper, was shot and killed by six Vallejo, California police officers who fired 55 rounds at him in 3.5 seconds on February 9, 2019, after he was found asleep behind the wheel of his car in a Taco Bell drive-thru with a handgun in his lap. Officers surrounded the vehicle; when McCoy stirred awake, they said he reached for the gun, and all six opened fire, striking him roughly 25 times. The Solano County District Attorney recused her office, and a special prosecutor concluded in January 2021 that all six officers acted in lawful self-defense. An independent use-of-force report commissioned by the city separately found the shooting “reasonable and necessary,” though the police chief internally recommended firing one of the six officers for unsafe firearm handling that endangered his colleagues — the only consequence any officer faced. No one has ever been criminally charged in McCoy's death.

name: Marcus-David Peters
summary: Marcus-David Peters, 24, a high school biology teacher, was shot and killed by Richmond, Virginia Police Officer Michael Nyantakyi on May 14, 2018, during a mental health crisis. Peters struck several vehicles with his car, crashed near an Interstate 95 ramp, then emerged naked and unarmed and ran into rush-hour highway traffic, where he was struck by a passing car. Body camera video showed him lying in the road, rolling and moving his limbs, before getting up and running toward Nyantakyi shouting threats; the officer deployed a Taser without effect, then fired his service weapon. Richmond's Commonwealth's Attorney found the shooting a “justifiable homicide” months later in 2018, and a successor prosecutor who reopened the case at the family's request reached the identical conclusion in 2020. No one has ever been charged in Peters's death, and his name has become a lasting symbol of Richmond's police reform movement.

name: Ronell Foster
summary: Ronell Foster, 33, a father of two, was shot and killed by Vallejo, California Police Officer Ryan McMahon on February 13, 2018, after McMahon tried to stop him for riding his bicycle without a headlight. Foster fled on foot after a chase; McMahon Tased him twice without effect, struck him repeatedly with a metal flashlight — including at least one blow to the head, which McMahon later admitted was a use of deadly force — and, after Foster grabbed the flashlight, shot him seven times, including once in the head and four times in the back. The Solano County District Attorney's Office cleared McMahon of criminal charges in January 2020, nearly two years later, finding the shooting justified. McMahon was the same officer who, thirteen months after killing Foster, was one of six Vallejo officers who fired 55 rounds at Willie McCoy in a Taco Bell drive-thru. No one has ever been charged in Foster's death.

name: Mansur Ball-Bey
summary: Mansur Ball-Bey, 18, was shot and killed by St. Louis Police Officers Kyle Chandler and Ronald Vaughan while they were serving a search warrant in the Fountain Park neighborhood on August 19, 2015. Police said Ball-Bey pointed a gun at officers as he ran out the back door of the home being searched; his family disputed he was armed at all. St. Louis Circuit Attorney Jennifer Joyce declined to charge either officer in June 2016, citing insufficient evidence to disprove self-defense. In February 2025, nearly a decade later, a federal jury in a wrongful death lawsuit rejected the officers' account, awarding Ball-Bey's family $18.75 million after deliberating for just 90 minutes. As of August 2025, the city still had not paid the judgment. No one has ever been criminally charged in Ball-Bey's death.

name: Stephon Watts
summary: Stephon Watts, 15, who was diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome and ADHD, was shot and killed in his own basement by Calumet City, Illinois police officers on February 1, 2012, after his father called the department's non-emergency line for help during an argument over school — following prior advice from social workers to call police when Stephon became agitated. Police had responded to the home at least ten times over the previous two years, and the address was flagged as belonging to a person with a disability. Officers said Stephon lunged at them with a steak knife; his father maintained it was only a butter knife. Two officers fired, killing him within roughly two minutes of entering the home. Cook County's State's Attorney cleared both officers of any misconduct that April, and a decade-long civil suit ended in 2022 when an Illinois appellate court ruled the officers were legally immune from liability. No officer was ever criminally charged, disciplined, or fired.

name: Dontre Hamilton
summary: Dontre Hamilton, 31, who had schizophrenia, was shot 13 or 14 times and killed by Milwaukee Police Officer Christopher Manney at Red Arrow Park on April 30, 2014, after Manney conducted a pat-down search while responding to a call about a man sleeping in the park. Manney said Hamilton grabbed his baton and attacked him, prompting him to open fire. Milwaukee County District Attorney John Chisholm declined to charge Manney in December 2014, finding the shooting was self-defense. The U.S. Department of Justice separately reviewed the case and declined federal charges in November 2015. Police Chief Edward Flynn fired Manney months before either declination — not for the shooting itself, but for conducting a pat-down that violated department policy and escalated the encounter; that firing was later upheld through two rounds of appeal. No one has ever been criminally charged in Hamilton's death.

name: Jerame Reid
summary: Jerame Reid, 36, was shot and killed by Bridgeton, New Jersey Police Officer Braheme Days on December 30, 2014, moments after Reid stepped out of a car with his hands raised during a traffic stop for running a stop sign. Dashcam video, released publicly in January 2015, showed Days and his partner Roger Worley ordering Reid to stay in the vehicle and not move; Reid exited anyway with his hands up, and Days opened fire, striking him fatally as Worley also fired but missed. A Cumberland County grand jury declined to indict either officer in May 2015. Federal prosecutors separately reviewed the case and announced in August 2016 that the evidence was insufficient to bring civil rights charges. No one has ever been charged in Reid's death.

name: Jamar Clark
summary: Jamar Clark, 24, was shot in the head by Minneapolis Police Officer Dustin Schwarze on November 15, 2015, during a struggle after officers responded to a report that Clark had assaulted his girlfriend and interfered with paramedics. Witnesses at the scene told police and reporters Clark was handcuffed when he was shot; the shooting sparked an 18-day protest encampment outside the police department's Fourth Precinct. Hennepin County Attorney Mike Freeman, bypassing the customary use of a grand jury, announced in March 2016 that DNA evidence and the absence of bruising on Clark's wrists showed he was not handcuffed and had grabbed at an officer's gun, and declined to bring charges. The U.S. Attorney's Office separately declined federal civil rights charges months later, and the police department cleared both officers of any policy violation. No one has ever been charged in Clark's death.

name: Jason Harrison
summary: Jason Harrison, 38, who had bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, was shot five times and killed by Dallas Police Officers John Rogers and Andrew Hutchins on June 14, 2014, within seconds of appearing in his own doorway holding a screwdriver. His mother, Shirley Harrison, had called 911 asking for trained officers to help take her son — off his medication and in crisis — to a hospital, and told the dispatcher he was bipolar and schizophrenic. Body camera footage, the first in Dallas to capture a fatal police shooting, showed officers ordering Harrison to drop the screwdriver before shooting him five times, twice in the back, as his mother screamed for them to stop. A Dallas County grand jury declined to indict either officer in April 2015, and a federal judge dismissed the family's civil rights lawsuit in 2016, ruling the shooting did not violate Harrison's constitutional rights. No one has ever been charged in Harrison's death.

name: Alfred Olango
summary: Alfred Olango, 38, a Ugandan refugee who had lived in the U.S. since childhood, was shot and killed by El Cajon, California Police Officer Richard Gonsalves on September 27, 2016, within about two minutes of officers arriving in response to his sister's 911 call reporting he was mentally ill, unarmed, and having an emotional breakdown after a close friend's death. Officers said Olango pulled an object from his pocket, assumed “what appeared to be a shooting stance,” and pointed it at Gonsalves, who fired four times as a second officer simultaneously deployed a Taser; the object turned out to be a vape pen. San Diego County District Attorney Bonnie Dumanis declined to charge Gonsalves in January 2017, finding the shooting legally justified. A 2019 civil jury also cleared Gonsalves of negligence. No one has ever been criminally charged in Olango's death.

name: India Kager
summary: India Kager, 27, a Navy veteran, mother, and U.S. Postal Service worker, was shot and killed by Virginia Beach SWAT officers on September 5, 2015, when they opened fire on her car in a 7-Eleven parking lot after her passenger, Angelo Perry — the father of her four-month-old son, who was in the backseat — fired at approaching officers. Police, who had been surveilling Perry as a homicide suspect, fired approximately 30 rounds into the vehicle within about nine seconds; Kager had no criminal history and no known involvement in Perry's activities. Her infant son survived uninjured. Virginia Beach's Commonwealth's Attorney declined to charge any of the four officers in March 2016, calling the shooting justified and confirming Kager herself was not engaged in any illegal activity. In 2018, a civil jury found two of the four officers liable for gross negligence, awarding her family $800,000. No one has ever been criminally charged in Kager's death.

name: Jayland Walker
summary: Jayland Walker, 25, was shot and killed by eight Akron, Ohio police officers on June 27, 2022, after fleeing a traffic stop for a broken taillight, firing a single shot from his car during the pursuit, then exiting and running on foot. Police said Walker, who was unarmed when he was shot, made a motion officers interpreted as reaching for a weapon; a gun was later found in his abandoned vehicle. The eight officers fired 94 shots in 6.7 seconds, striking Walker with 46 entrance or graze wounds, including several in the back, according to the county medical examiner. A special grand jury seated by Ohio's attorney general declined to indict any of the officers in April 2023, finding their use of force legally justified. The city later paid Walker's family a $4.8 million settlement. No one has ever been criminally charged in Walker's death.

name: Ta'Kiya Young
summary: Ta'Kiya Young, 21, seven months pregnant with her third child, was shot and killed by Blendon Township, Ohio Police Officer Connor Grubb on August 24, 2023, in a Kroger parking lot after being accused of shoplifting alcohol. Body camera footage showed Grubb standing in front of Young's car as she slowly rolled it forward attempting to leave; he fired a single shot through the windshield, killing her and her unborn daughter. A Franklin County grand jury indicted Grubb on murder, felonious assault, and involuntary manslaughter charges in August 2024, a year after the shooting. On November 21, 2025, following a roughly two-week trial, a jury acquitted Grubb of all six charges after about 6.5 hours of deliberation, finding his use of force objectively reasonable given the moving vehicle. No one has ever been convicted in Young's death.

name: Patrick Lyoya
summary: Patrick Lyoya, 26, a Congolese refugee, was shot in the back of the head by Grand Rapids, Michigan Police Officer Christopher Schurr during a traffic stop on April 4, 2022. Lyoya ran after Schurr pulled him over for a mismatched license plate; Schurr caught him, and the two struggled over Schurr's Taser for roughly two and a half minutes before Schurr, straddling Lyoya face-down on the ground, fired a single shot into the back of his head. Schurr was fired and charged with second-degree murder in June 2022, becoming one of the few Michigan officers ever criminally charged for an on-duty killing. After a three-year legal battle, his trial began in April 2025; a jury deliberated over 20 hours across four days before deadlocking, and a mistrial was declared on May 8, 2025. Kent County's prosecutor announced on May 22, 2025 that he would not seek a retrial, concluding a second trial was unlikely to produce a different result. No one has ever been convicted in Lyoya's death.

name: Rayshard Brooks
summary: Rayshard Brooks, 27, was shot and killed by Atlanta Police Officer Garrett Rolfe outside a Wendy's restaurant on June 12, 2020, after a struggle that began when officers tried to arrest him for driving under the influence. Brooks resisted, grabbed a Taser from Officer Devin Brosnan, and ran; an autopsy found he was shot twice in the back. Then-Fulton County District Attorney Paul Howard charged Rolfe with felony murder within days, less than three weeks after George Floyd's killing sparked nationwide protests. Howard lost his re-election bid months later, and the case was passed between three successive prosecutors before a special prosecutor appointed by Georgia's attorney general dismissed all charges against both officers in August 2022, finding the shooting objectively reasonable. Rolfe, initially fired, was reinstated with back pay by the city's Civil Service Board. No one has ever been convicted in Brooks's death.

name: Amir Locke
summary: Amir Locke, 22, an aspiring hip-hop artist, was shot and killed by Minneapolis Police SWAT Officer Mark Hanneman on February 2, 2022, within about ten seconds of officers using a key to enter his cousin's apartment on a no-knock warrant tied to a homicide investigation in neighboring St. Paul. Locke, asleep on the couch under a blanket, was not named in the warrant and was not a suspect in the investigation. Body camera video showed him stirring awake and rising with a handgun he was legally licensed to carry as officers shouted commands; Hanneman shot him three times, saying Locke had pointed the gun toward officers, a characterization Locke's family disputed. Minnesota's attorney general and the Hennepin County attorney jointly announced in April 2022 that there was insufficient evidence to charge Hanneman. No one has ever been charged in Locke's death.

name: Andrew Brown Jr.
summary: Andrew Brown Jr., 42, a father of seven, was shot and killed by Pasquotank County, North Carolina sheriff's deputies on April 21, 2021, while sitting in his car as they attempted to serve felony drug arrest and search warrants at his home in Elizabeth City. Three of the seven deputies present fired 14 shots as Brown's car pulled away; he was killed by a shot to the back of the head. He was unarmed, and no weapon was found in his vehicle. District Attorney Andrew Womble announced on May 18, 2021 — the day after a jury convicted Derek Chauvin of murdering George Floyd — that the shooting was "justified" because Brown's car had made contact with a deputy, and declined to bring any charges. Brown's family, reviewing the same body camera footage, said he never posed a threat and was "executed" while trying to drive away. No one has ever been charged in Brown's death.

name: Aiyana Stanley-Jones
summary: Aiyana Stanley-Jones, 7, was shot in the head and killed by Detroit Police Special Response Team Officer Joseph Weekley just after midnight on May 16, 2010, as she slept on a couch next to her grandmother during a raid on their home in search of a murder suspect who did not live there. The raid, being filmed for the A&E reality show "The First 48," began with another officer throwing a flash-bang grenade through the window; Weekley, first through the door, said his gun fired when the girl's grandmother, Mertilla Jones, struck it during a struggle, which she denied under oath. Weekley was charged with involuntary manslaughter and careless discharge of a firearm. His first trial ended in a hung jury in 2013; a judge later dismissed the manslaughter charge outright during his second trial in 2014, and that jury deadlocked on the remaining misdemeanor count as well, resulting in a second mistrial. Prosecutors declined to pursue a third trial, and all charges were formally dropped in January 2015. No one has ever been convicted in Aiyana's death.

name: Aura Rosser
summary: Aura Rosser, 40, an artist and mother of three who was living with addiction, was shot and killed by Ann Arbor, Michigan Police Officer David Ried in her home in the early morning hours of November 10, 2014, within five to ten seconds of officers entering the house. Her boyfriend, Victor Stephens, had called police to report a domestic dispute and asked them to remove Rosser from the home, but said afterward that lethal force was not justified. Police said Rosser approached officers with a knife; Officer Mark Raab fired a Taser at the same moment Ried fired his handgun, striking her once in the chest. The Washtenaw County Prosecutor's Office declined to charge Ried in January 2015, finding the shooting lawful self-defense. No one has ever been charged in Rosser's death.

name: Terrance Kellom
summary: Terrance Kellom, 20, was shot and killed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Officer Mitchell Quinn on April 27, 2015, at his father's Detroit home, in front of his family, as a multi-agency federal fugitive task force served an arrest warrant on an armed-robbery charge. Quinn said Kellom, who had hidden in an attic, dropped down and lunged at him with a hammer, forcing him to fire; Kellom's father maintained his son died with clenched fists and no hammer. Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy declined to charge Quinn in August 2015, citing blood-spatter evidence she said supported his account. Nearly four years later, during sworn deposition testimony in the family's federal lawsuit, a Detroit police officer who had witnessed the shooting and originally corroborated the hammer account testified he could no longer recall seeing a hammer at all. No one has ever been charged in Kellom's death.

name: Kendrec McDade
summary: Kendrec McDade, 19, a college student, was shot seven times and killed by Pasadena, California Police Officers Jeffrey Newlen and Matthew Griffin on March 24, 2012, after they chased him down a residential street responding to a 911 call describing an armed robbery. The caller, Oscar Carrillo, had lied about the robbers being armed and mentioned a gun eight times to get a faster police response; his backpack had in fact been stolen from his car in an unarmed burglary. McDade, who was unarmed, was shot while reportedly reaching toward his waistband as he ran. He was left handcuffed on the ground for roughly eight minutes before paramedics arrived, his last words reportedly "Why did they shoot me?" The Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office cleared both officers of criminal wrongdoing in December 2012, finding they acted in lawful self-defense. Carrillo separately pleaded guilty to two misdemeanor counts of filing a false police report, receiving 90 days in jail — the only criminal conviction connected to the case. No officer has ever been charged in McDade's death.

name: Miles Hall
summary: Miles Hall, 23, who had schizophrenia, was shot four times and killed by Walnut Creek, California Police Officers KC Hsiao and Melissa Murphy on June 2, 2019, during a mental health crisis near his home. His mother, Taun Hall, had called and left a voicemail with a Walnut Creek officer the day before, warning that her son was having "another episode" and asking them to be prepared. When officers responded to reports Hall was carrying a nearly 5-foot steel digging tool and had chased a vehicle on foot, they deployed a beanbag shotgun first; when that failed to stop him, Hsiao and Murphy shot him. The Contra Costa County District Attorney's Office announced in May 2021, nearly two years later, that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute either officer. No one has ever been charged in Hall's death.

name: Jonathan Sanders
summary: Jonathan Sanders, 39, a horse trainer, died on July 8, 2015 in Stonewall, Mississippi after an encounter with police officer Kevin Herrington that witnesses said involved a chokehold lasting as long as 20 to 30 minutes. Sanders had been riding a horse-drawn buggy near a gas station when he intervened in an argument between Herrington and another man he knew; witnesses said Herrington's patrol lights startled Sanders's horse, throwing him to the ground, after which Herrington grabbed him and restrained him on the ground. Multiple witnesses told the family's attorneys Herrington said he was "going to get that [racial slur]" before the confrontation and that Sanders repeatedly said "I can't breathe" before he died at the scene. A grand jury declined to indict Herrington in January 2016, and a second grand jury concluded in March 2016 that Sanders had choked to death after swallowing cocaine he was trying to hide, finding no excessive force was used. No one has ever been charged in Sanders's death.

name: Tyre King
summary: Tyre King, 13, was shot and killed by Columbus, Ohio Police Officer Bryan Mason on September 14, 2016, during a foot chase after officers responded to a report of an armed $10 robbery. Mason said King pulled a BB gun with an attached laser sight from his waistband during the chase, prompting him to fire; an older teenager who had been with King, Demetrious Braxton, later told the Columbus Dispatch that King was running away, not reaching for anything, when he was shot. A Franklin County grand jury declined to indict Mason — who had been involved in three prior fatal or use-of-force shootings before this one — in May 2017. A federal jury separately cleared Mason of civil liability in 2023, after the judge excluded testimony about Mason's history of 47 use-of-force reports in the seven years preceding King's death. No one has ever been charged in King's death.

name: John Neville
summary: John Neville, 56, died on December 4, 2019, three days after Forsyth County, North Carolina jail detention officers restrained him face-down on the floor of his cell in a "bent-leg prone restraint" for nearly an hour. Body camera video showed Neville, who had fallen from his top bunk during an apparent seizure, saying "I can't breathe" and calling out for his deceased mother more than 25 times while restrained; officers responded at least twice with "if you can talk, you can breathe." A medical examiner ruled the death a homicide from positional and compressional asphyxia. Five detention officers and a jail nurse were charged with involuntary manslaughter in 2020; a grand jury declined to indict any of the five officers in April 2022, indicting only the nurse, Michelle Heughins — whose attorney argued she was the only person present who tried to save Neville's life. In 2023, at the Neville family's own request, prosecutors dropped the remaining charge against Heughins as well. No one has ever been convicted in Neville's death.

name: Ronald Greene
summary: Ronald Greene, 49, died on May 10, 2019, following a high-speed chase and arrest by Louisiana State Police troopers outside Monroe, Louisiana. Authorities initially told his family he died from injuries sustained when his car crashed at the end of the chase. Body camera video, suppressed for two years until an Associated Press investigation obtained and published it in 2021, instead showed troopers stunning Greene with Tasers, punching him, and dragging him by his ankle shackles face-down on the ground while he pleaded, "I'm scared! I'm your brother!" Five officers were eventually indicted in 2022 on charges ranging from negligent homicide to malfeasance. By 2024, prosecutors had dropped the most serious charges against every defendant; the lead trooper avoided trial entirely by pleading no contest to a single misdemeanor battery charge in exchange for probation. The Department of Justice separately declined to bring federal charges. No one has ever been convicted of a felony in Greene's death.

name: Alonzo Smith
summary: Alonzo Smith, 27, died on November 1, 2015 after being restrained and handcuffed by two privately employed "special police officers" at Marbury Plaza apartments in Southeast Washington, D.C. Neighbors reported hearing Smith, who was shirtless and barefoot, running and screaming that someone was trying to kill him before the special officers caught him, put him in a bear hug, and held him face-down on the ground. When Metropolitan Police arrived, Smith was found handcuffed, unconscious, and not breathing; he died at a hospital soon after. The D.C. medical examiner classified his death a homicide. Nearly a year later, the U.S. Attorney's Office announced there was insufficient evidence to charge either special officer, attributing Smith's death to a cocaine-related cardiac event that restraint may have contributed to, rather than to excessive force. No one has ever been charged in Smith's death, and the special officers involved have never been publicly identified.

name: Darius Tarver
summary: Darius Tarver, 23, a University of North Texas criminal justice student and member of the National Organization of Black Law Enforcement, was shot and killed by a Denton, Texas police officer on January 21, 2020, outside his apartment. Just a week earlier, Tarver had suffered a traumatic brain injury in a car crash and been released from the ICU; his family said he began exhibiting significant mental impairment afterward. His roommate called police for help after Tarver barricaded himself in his room, muttering about God and light. Body camera video showed him holding a frying pan and a large knife when four officers arrived; after he was Tased twice without effect and continued to advance, one officer opened fire. A Denton County grand jury declined to indict the officer, whose name was never publicly released, in March 2021. An internal department review separately found no policy violations. No one has ever been charged in Tarver's death.

name: Chinedu Okobi
summary: Chinedu Okobi, 36, a Morehouse College graduate and father, died on October 3, 2018 after San Mateo County, California sheriff's deputies Tased him repeatedly, struck him with a baton, and pepper-sprayed him during a confrontation that began when a deputy approached him for jaywalking on El Camino Real in Millbrae. Okobi crossed the street to get away from the deputy; when more deputies arrived, a violent struggle followed in which he was shocked with a Taser seven times. He went into cardiac arrest and died; an autopsy attributed his death to cardiac arrest linked to an undiagnosed enlarged heart, physical exertion, restraint, and the repeated Taser shocks. San Mateo County District Attorney Steve Wagstaffe announced in March 2019 that none of the five deputies and sergeant involved would face criminal charges. Okobi was the third person with mental illness to die after being Tased by law enforcement in San Mateo County within that same year. No one has ever been charged in Okobi's death.

name: Osaze Osagie
summary: Osaze Osagie, 29, who had schizophrenia and Asperger's syndrome, was shot and killed by a State College, Pennsylvania police officer on March 20, 2019, at his apartment while three officers attempted to serve a mental health warrant his own father had requested. Sylvester Osagie, worried about his son's deteriorating condition, had asked police for an involuntary commitment warrant after his son sent a text threatening self-harm. When officers arrived, Osagie reportedly ran at them holding a steak knife; one officer fired three shots, striking him once in the shoulder and twice in the back as he turned. It was the first fatal police shooting in the department's 103-year history. Centre County District Attorney Bernie Cantorna announced in May 2019, after a six-week investigation, that the officer would face no charges, finding the shooting justified. A federal judge dismissed the family's civil lawsuit in 2023. No one has ever been charged in Osagie's death.

name: Julian Lewis
summary: Julian Edward Roosevelt Lewis, 60, a semi-retired carpenter, was shot in the face and killed by Georgia State Patrol Trooper Jacob Thompson on a rural road in Screven County, Georgia, on August 7, 2020, after Thompson tried to stop him over a broken taillight. When Lewis did not immediately stop, Thompson performed a PIT maneuver that forced his car into a ditch, then shot him once, unarmed, within about two seconds of getting out of his own patrol car. Thompson wrote in his report that Lewis had been revving his engine and turning the wheel as if trying to ram him — a claim a Georgia Bureau of Investigation agent later testified was physically impossible, since the crash had disconnected Lewis's car battery, leaving the vehicle inoperable.
