Thompson was fired and charged with felony murder days later, but a Screven County grand jury declined to indict him in June 2021. No one has ever been convicted in Lewis's death.

name: Emantic “E.J.” Bradford Jr.
summary: Emantic “E.J.” Bradford Jr., 21, was shot three times from behind and killed by Hoover, Alabama Police Officer David Alexander at the Riverchase Galleria mall on Thanksgiving night, November 22, 2018, moments after another man opened fire during an altercation, wounding an 18-year-old and a 12-year-old bystander. Bradford, who held a valid permit to carry, was seen on surveillance video running toward the wounded with his gun drawn; witnesses and his family's attorney said he was trying to help, not attack anyone. Hoover police initially publicly identified Bradford himself as the shooter, then retracted that within a day. Alabama's attorney general took over the case from the local district attorney, citing conflicts of interest, and announced in February 2019 that the officer had mistakenly believed Bradford fired the earlier shots but was still legally justified in killing him regardless. The FBI separately found no basis for federal civil rights charges. No one has ever been charged in Bradford's death.

name: Kayla Moore
summary: Kayla Moore, 41, a Black transgender woman living with schizophrenia, died in Berkeley, California police custody on February 12, 2013, after up to six officers restrained her face-down on a futon in her own apartment. Her roommate had called police asking for a mental health welfare check, not an arrest; officers instead learned of an outstanding warrant — later found to have actually been issued for a different person who shared her legal name — and moved to take her into custody. During the struggle to restrain her, Moore stopped breathing and could not be revived. A Berkeley police sergeant's internal report ruled the death accidental and the force used reasonable within three months. No criminal charges were ever sought against any officer. A federal judge dismissed the family's civil rights lawsuit in 2016, and the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld that dismissal in 2020, finding the officers had not used excessive force. No one has ever been held accountable in Moore's death.

name: Steven Taylor
summary: Steven Taylor, 33, was shot and killed by San Leandro, California Police Officer Jason Fletcher inside a Walmart on April 18, 2020, after being reported for shoplifting while holding an aluminum baseball bat. Body camera video showed that within about 40 seconds of Fletcher's arrival, he Tased Taylor twice and then fired a single fatal round into his chest; Taylor's family said he was suffering a mental health crisis, not posing a deadly threat. Fletcher was charged with voluntary manslaughter in 2021, becoming a rare case of an officer criminally charged in California for an on-duty shooting. After more than five years of delays, prosecutorial turnover, and disputes over withheld evidence, Alameda County's district attorney moved to drop the charges in December 2025, and a judge dismissed the case just weeks before it was finally set to go to trial. No one has ever been convicted in Taylor's death.

name: De'Von Bailey
summary: De'Von Bailey, 19, was shot and killed by Colorado Springs Police Officers Blake Evenson and Sgt. Alan Van't Land on August 3, 2019, while running away from officers investigating a report of an armed robbery. Body camera video, later released publicly, showed officers firing eight shots total, striking Bailey three times in the back and once in the arm as he fled; officers said he had reached for a firearm, but the released footage does not clearly show him pulling a weapon from his pocket before the shooting began. A gun was recovered at the scene. Fourth Judicial District Attorney Dan May referred the case to a grand jury rather than deciding himself, and in November 2019 the grand jury found the officers' use of force justified, declining to indict either of them. The city later paid Bailey's family nearly $3 million to settle a federal civil rights lawsuit alleging racial profiling, without admitting wrongdoing. No one has ever been charged in Bailey's death.

name: Antwon Rose II
summary: Antwon Rose II, 17, was shot three times — in the back, arm, and side of the face — and killed by East Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania Police Officer Michael Rosfeld on June 19, 2018, as he ran from a car that had been pulled over minutes after a drive-by shooting elsewhere. Rose, unarmed, fled along with another passenger while the driver was being arrested; bystander cellphone video captured the shooting. Rosfeld was charged with criminal homicide — he had been sworn in as an East Pittsburgh officer only hours before the shooting, following prior stints at other departments. At trial in March 2019, a jury that included three Black jurors deliberated fewer than four hours before acquitting Rosfeld of all charges, including first-degree murder, third-degree murder, voluntary manslaughter, and involuntary manslaughter. No one has ever been convicted in Rose's death.

name: Angelo Crooms & Sincere Pierce
summary: Angelo “AJ” Crooms, 16, and Sincere Pierce, 18, were shot and killed by Brevard County, Florida Sheriff's Deputy Jafet Santiago-Miranda on November 13, 2020, in a Cocoa driveway during an attempted stop of a car deputies believed, based on a report that later proved incorrect, had been stolen. Dashcam video showed the deputy approaching with his gun drawn, repeatedly yelling for the car to stop; Crooms, who was driving, backed up slightly then drove forward, and the deputy opened fire, killing both teens. A third occupant survived uninjured. The family's attorneys said the video showed the car moving away from the deputy, not toward him, and that deputies never confirmed the car was actually stolen before drawing weapons. Brevard County State Attorney Phil Archer announced in April 2021 — the day after Derek Chauvin's murder conviction — that no charges would be filed. No one has ever been charged in either teen's death.

name: Terrence Sterling
summary: Terrence Sterling, 31, was shot and killed by Metropolitan Police Department Officer Brian Trainer in Washington, D.C. in the early morning hours of September 11, 2016, after officers blocked his motorcycle with their cruiser following a high-speed chase. Trainer said Sterling revved his motorcycle and rammed it into the cruiser's door, pinning his leg, forcing him to fire twice through the window; an internal MPD investigator later testified he doubted Trainer's account, and the department's own review board found Trainer was not in danger and had no reason to draw his weapon at all. Trainer had not activated his body camera until one to three minutes after the shooting, violating department policy. Federal prosecutors declined to bring charges in August 2017. D.C.'s MPD trial board recommended firing Trainer months later for the unjustified shooting, and the police chief fired him in 2018 after his appeal was denied — an administrative outcome, not a criminal one. No one has ever been criminally charged in Sterling's death.

name: Jamee Johnson
summary: Jamee Johnson, 22, a Florida A&M University student, was shot and killed by Jacksonville Sheriff's Officer Josue Garriga during a traffic stop for a seatbelt violation on December 14, 2019. Body camera footage showed Johnson telling Garriga he had a legally owned handgun in the car; after Garriga asked him to step out, Johnson dove back into the vehicle, a struggle followed, and Garriga shot him four times, with video capturing Johnson begging for his life. Garriga said Johnson was reaching for the gun; the family's attorney argued the autopsy's bullet trajectories contradicted that account. Florida's State Attorney's Office concluded in July 2020 that the shooting was justified, declining to bring charges. The city later settled a federal civil lawsuit with Johnson's family for $200,000, without admitting wrongdoing. In 2024, Garriga was separately arrested and charged with child sex crimes unrelated to the shooting. No one has ever been charged in Johnson's death.

name: Dreasjon “Sean” Reed
summary: Dreasjon “Sean” Reed, 21, a former U.S. Air Force airman and legal gun owner, was shot and killed by Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department Officer Dejoure Mercer on May 6, 2020, at the end of a high-speed chase Reed livestreamed on Facebook to thousands of viewers in real time. The chase itself had been called off by IMPD's own chief for being too dangerous; Mercer, on foot, caught up to Reed after he parked and ran. The livestream's shaky camera captured the sound of a Taser and then gunshots, but never showed the shooting itself clearly, and no body camera or dashcam footage of the moment existed. Police said Reed fired at Mercer first; his family's attorney said he never had a gun in his hand at all. A detective who later walked past Reed's body was recorded joking it would be a “closed casket” and was internally disciplined for it. A special grand jury declined to indict Mercer in November 2020, six months after the shooting. No one has ever been charged in Reed's death.

name: Kajuan Raye
summary: Kajuan Raye, 19, was shot in the back and killed by Chicago Police Sergeant John Poulos during a foot chase in the Englewood neighborhood on November 23, 2016, after Poulos believed Raye matched the description of a battery suspect. Poulos said Raye twice pointed a gun at him during the chase; no weapon was found at the scene despite an extensive search, and released surveillance video does not show Raye turning toward Poulos with anything in his hand. Three months later, a resident reported finding a handgun in the bushes near where Raye was shot. Chicago's Civilian Office of Police Accountability ruled the shooting justified in 2019, concluding circumstantial and social media evidence made it “likely and reasonable” the gun was Raye's. No criminal charges were ever filed. It was the second time Poulos had fatally shot someone; he had also killed an unarmed man in 2013 and was cleared both times. No one has ever been criminally charged in Raye's death.

name: Walter Wallace Jr.
summary: Walter Wallace Jr., 27, a father with bipolar disorder, was shot 14 times and killed by Philadelphia Police Officers Sean Matarazzo and Thomas Munz outside his family's Cobbs Creek home on October 26, 2020, less than a minute after they arrived. His family had called 911 seeking an ambulance during a mental health crisis; officers instead confronted him with guns drawn as he held a knife, and one was heard on body camera telling the other “shoot him” roughly six seconds before both fired. His mother tried to position herself between her son and the officers while pleading with them not to shoot. District Attorney Larry Krasner personally led the investigation but never filed criminal charges against either officer. The city settled a wrongful death lawsuit with the family for $2.5 million in 2021. Wallace's own family did not call for murder charges, saying instead that officers lacked the training and less-lethal tools — neither carried a Taser — to handle a mental health crisis without killing him. No one has ever been charged in Wallace's death.

name: Byron Williams
summary: Byron Williams, 50, died on September 5, 2019, after Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Officers Patrick Campbell and Benjamin Vasquez stopped him for riding his bicycle without a safety light near Martin Luther King Boulevard, chased him after he fled, and restrained him face-down on the ground with a knee on his back. Body camera footage showed Williams saying “I can't breathe” 24 times while handcuffed; when he told officers he couldn't breathe, one replied, “because you're f---ing tired from running.” He went limp and died after being transported. The Clark County Coroner's Office ruled his death a homicide, citing prone restraint as a contributing condition alongside methamphetamine use and pre-existing heart and lung disease. District Attorney Steve Wolfson declined to file charges against any officer in 2020. Two officers were disciplined internally, and both later returned to active duty. No one has ever been criminally charged in Williams's death.

name: Michael Dean
summary: Michael Dean, 32, a father of three, was shot in the head and killed by Temple, Texas Police Officer Carmen DeCruz during a traffic stop on December 2, 2019, after DeCruz pursued him for speeding. According to the arrest affidavit, Dean eventually stopped his car; DeCruz approached with his gun drawn and, reaching into the vehicle to grab the keys from the ignition, pulled the trigger. Dean was unarmed. DeCruz was charged with second-degree manslaughter and criminally negligent homicide. After a roughly two-week trial in February 2023, a Bell County jury deliberated about two hours before acquitting DeCruz of both charges; his attorney argued Dean, who was legally intoxicated at .2 blood alcohol content, “caused his own death” by resisting and touching the gun. Dean's family disputes that account. No one has ever been convicted in Dean's death.

name: Marvin Scott III
summary: Marvin Scott III, 26, who had schizophrenia, died in custody at the Collin County, Texas jail on March 14, 2021, nine months after George Floyd's murder, after detention officers strapped him to a restraint bed, pepper-sprayed him, and covered his face with a spit hood. He had been arrested that afternoon for possessing less than two ounces of marijuana and was medically cleared at a hospital before being taken to jail, where he began exhibiting what the sheriff called “strange behavior.” Security video released by the county showed him struggling for roughly 17 minutes while restrained before going unresponsive; officers then removed the hood and began CPR. The county medical examiner ruled his death a homicide, citing “a fatal acute stress response” during the restraint struggle. A Collin County grand jury declined to indict any of the eight jailers involved in June 2021. No one has ever been charged in Scott's death.

name: Jamycheal Mitchell
summary: Jamycheal Mitchell, 24, who had schizoaffective disorder, died on August 19, 2015 in his cell at the Hampton Roads Regional Jail in Portsmouth, Virginia, roughly four months after his arrest for allegedly stealing about $5 worth of snacks — a Mountain Dew, a Snickers bar, and a Zebra Cake — from a 7-Eleven. A judge twice ordered him transferred to a state mental hospital for competency restoration treatment; clerical errors meant his name was never placed on the hospital's waiting list, and the transfer never happened. He spent 100 days in restrictive housing, was allegedly struck on the knuckles with a flashlight and mocked by correctional officers, and lost 46 pounds before he was found dead, in a cell smeared with feces, of heart failure accompanied by “wasting syndrome.” After a years-long investigation, the Portsmouth Commonwealth's Attorney's Office released a 166-page report in 2019 calling his death “tragic and likely avoidable” but concluded no charges could be sought due to missing information. No one has ever been charged in Mitchell's death.

name: Natasha McKenna
summary: Natasha McKenna, 37, a mother diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, died on February 8, 2015, five days after six Fairfax County, Virginia sheriff's deputies in biohazard suits and riot gear shocked her with a Taser four times while extracting her, naked and shackled, from her cell at the Fairfax County Adult Detention Center. She had been held for over a week awaiting transfer on an outstanding warrant; video of the extraction captured her saying, “You promised you wouldn't kill me.” She went into cardiac arrest during the struggle and never regained consciousness. Fairfax County's top prosecutor announced in September 2015 that no deputy would be charged, calling her death a “tragic accident,” and the state medical examiner ruled it accidental, attributing it to excited delirium linked to the restraints and stun gun. No one has ever been criminally charged in McKenna's death.

name: Deon Kay
summary: Deon Kay, 18, was shot and killed by Metropolitan Police Department Officer Alexander Alvarez in Southeast Washington, D.C. on September 2, 2020, roughly six seconds after Alvarez got out of his squad car pursuing a group of men reported to be brandishing guns. Body camera footage showed Kay running, then turning toward Alvarez with a gun in his hand a moment before Alvarez fired once, striking him in the chest; the gun was later found roughly 98 feet away, and it remains disputed whether Kay tossed it or the bullet's impact knocked it from his hand. Federal prosecutors declined criminal civil rights charges in November 2020, and the D.C. Auditor's office separately found the shooting legally justified as self-defense while concluding officers had “squandered” chances to de-escalate. Nearly five years later, in July 2025, a civil jury found Alvarez liable for wrongful death, negligence, and battery, awarding Kay's mother $655,000; the city fought to overturn or reduce that verdict before settling for a lesser amount in 2026. No one has ever been criminally charged in Kay's death.

name: Mickel Lewis Sr.
summary: Mickel Lewis Sr., 39, a father of seven, was shot and killed by Kern County, California Sheriff's Deputy Jason Ayala during a traffic stop in Mojave on October 2, 2020. Ayala had been surveilling Lewis based on a confidential informant's tip that he possessed a gun while on probation; a pat-down found no weapon. The sheriff's office said Lewis then ran to his car, reached under the seat, and charged at Ayala with his hand in his waistband, prompting Ayala to fire five shots, two striking Lewis in the back. No gun was found on or near Lewis; a handgun was later recovered behind a utility pole where a passenger from his car had been seen. An internal sheriff's review board found Ayala acted within department policy and returned him to duty within weeks. No criminal charges were ever filed. In March 2025, a federal jury in Fresno unanimously awarded Lewis's family $30.5 million, finding Ayala used excessive and unreasonable force and was negligent — the second-largest jury verdict for a police shooting in California history. No one has ever been criminally charged in Lewis's death.

name: Alteria Woods
summary: Alteria Woods, 21, a pharmacy technician, was shot 10 times and killed while lying in bed when three Indian River County, Florida SWAT officers fired into the bedroom during a pre-dawn drug raid on March 19, 2017. The raid targeted her boyfriend's father; a gunfight broke out between her boyfriend, Andrew Coffee IV, and the officers after Coffee said he did not know they were law enforcement. A grand jury exonerated all three officers who fired — finding no probable cause to indict any of them — and instead indicted Coffee himself for Woods's murder, under a legal theory that his actions had caused the deadly police response. A jury acquitted Coffee of murder and every violent charge against him in 2021, convicting him only of a firearm-possession charge unrelated to the shooting itself. No one has ever been convicted of killing Alteria Woods.

name: DeJuan Guillory
summary: DeJuan Guillory, 27, was shot three times and killed by Evangeline Parish, Louisiana Sheriff's Deputy Paul — also reported as Holden — Lafleur on a rural road near Mamou on July 6, 2017, after the deputy stopped the ATV Guillory was riding with his girlfriend. A struggle followed the stop; the deputy said Guillory struck him and knocked him briefly unconscious before Guillory's girlfriend, DeQuince Brown, jumped on his back trying to grab his gun. Brown's attorney said Guillory was already lying face-down, being handcuffed with one hand behind his back, when the deputy fired the first of six shots; witnesses agree only two people were present to see exactly what happened. Brown was initially charged with attempted first-degree murder of a police officer, later reduced to lesser charges. A grand jury declined to indict Lafleur in December 2017. No one has ever been charged in Guillory's death.

name: Tommie McGlothen Jr.
summary: Tommie McGlothen Jr., 44, who had a documented mental health condition, died in the backseat of a Shreveport, Louisiana police vehicle on April 5, 2020, following the third of three encounters with officers that day. Cellphone and body camera video showed officers striking McGlothen, including an elbow blow to his neck, and using a Taser and pepper spray on him before forcing him, limp, into the back of a patrol car; witnesses said he then sat unattended for roughly 40 to 48 minutes before paramedics checked on him. The Caddo Parish coroner ruled the death natural but “possibly preventable” due to the delay in medical attention. Four officers were indicted on negligent homicide and malfeasance charges; all four waived a jury and were acquitted by a judge in June 2022 after the defense's motion for a directed verdict was granted when the prosecution rested its case. No one has ever been convicted in McGlothen's death.

name: Willie Tillman
summary: Willie Sherman Tillman, 33, a father of three, died on May 9, 2016, eighteen days after being shot four times by Fayetteville, Arkansas Police Officer Brandon Jones during a traffic stop that turned into a struggle inside Tillman's moving vehicle. Police said Tillman re-entered his car after being asked to step out, and that officers used Tasers on him without effect before the car began moving with Officer Jones still inside; police characterized Tillman's driving as having dragged the two officers, justifying the shooting. Both the Fayetteville Police Department's internal investigation and the Washington County prosecutor concluded the shooting was justified, lawful, and within department policy. Jones returned to duty after three weeks of paid leave. Tillman was the second Black man in recent memory shot and killed by Fayetteville police, following the earlier fatal shooting of a white man in an unrelated incident that the department also ruled justified. No one has ever been charged in Tillman's death.

name: Christopher Whitfield
summary: Christopher Lee Whitfield, 31, who had schizophrenia, was shot and killed by East Feliciana Parish, Louisiana Deputy Glenn Sims Sr. outside a gas station in Ethel on October 14, 2019, after Whitfield allegedly took raw chicken and a carton of eggs from an outdoor cooler and fled on foot. Sims fired a warning shot into the ground during the chase, then caught Whitfield and scuffled with him on the ground; the sheriff's office said Sims's gun discharged accidentally during the struggle, striking Whitfield in the lower back and killing him. Days later, Sheriff Jeff Travis publicly acknowledged Sims had a prior criminal record including illegal discharge of a firearm, simple battery, and resisting an officer, none of which had been known to him. A grand jury twice considered the case and, on its second sitting in March 2020, declined to indict Sims on second-degree murder. Sims remained a commissioned deputy years afterward despite not returning to active duty. No one has ever been charged in Whitfield's death.

name: Thurman Blevins
summary: Thurman Blevins, 31, was shot and killed by Minneapolis Police Officers Justin Schmidt and Ryan Kelly on June 23, 2018, at the end of a roughly 40-second foot chase in a north Minneapolis alley. A 911 caller had reported a man matching Blevins's description firing a handgun into the air and the ground; officers spotted him with a gun in his waistband, and he ran when they approached. Officers said Blevins pulled the gun from his pocket and turned toward them during the chase, prompting them to fire 14 shots, four of which struck him. Hennepin County Attorney Mike Freeman announced in July 2018, after a five-week investigation, that the shooting was legally authorized and declined to bring charges against either officer. Body camera video of the shooting was released to the public only the night before that announcement. No one has ever been charged in Blevins's death.

name: George Tillman III
summary: George Homer Tillman III, 32, a licensed electrician and father of five visiting family from Maryland, was shot and killed by NYPD officers in South Ozone Park, Queens, on April 17, 2016, after being approached over an open container of alcohol outside a double-parked vehicle. Tillman complied by handing off the bottle, but police said he then ran when officers moved to question him, and that he pointed a loaded .40-caliber pistol at an officer during the chase; four of five pursuing officers opened fire, striking him approximately 13 times. Queens District Attorney Richard Brown cleared the officers of any wrongdoing in October 2016 after a six-month, 71-page investigation, finding Tillman's DNA on the recovered gun. No non-police witness ever corroborated that Tillman was armed, and a companion who was present was held in police custody for 12 hours without charge and without access to an attorney. In 2025, nine years after the shooting, a federal jury found NYPD officers liable in the family's wrongful death lawsuit and awarded $6.3 million. No one has ever been criminally charged in Tillman's death.

name: Charleena Lyles
summary: Charleena Lyles, 30, a pregnant mother of four, was shot seven times and killed by Seattle Police Officers Jason Anderson and Steven McNew inside her Magnuson Park apartment on Father's Day, June 18, 2017, after she called 911 herself to report a burglary. Officers said Lyles's demeanor suddenly shifted and she produced a knife, lunging at Anderson and missing his stomach by inches, prompting both officers to open fire; neither carried a Taser at the time. A King County inquest jury unanimously found the shooting justified in 2022, though it also found the officers had not followed department policy on using a stun gun. King County Prosecutor Dan Satterberg declined to file charges weeks later, citing insufficient evidence to disprove justifiable homicide, while acknowledging the case “does not mean everything was done right.” The city settled a wrongful death lawsuit with Lyles's family for $3.5 million in 2021. No one has ever been charged in Lyles's death.

name: Miles Jackson
summary: Miles Jackson, 27, was shot 20 times and killed inside an emergency room at Mount Carmel St. Ann's Hospital in Westerville, Ohio on April 12, 2021, during a struggle with Columbus police officers who had come to arrest him on outstanding warrants after he was brought in for a suspected overdose. An earlier pat-down by Westerville police had missed a handgun concealed in his pants pocket; when Columbus officers attempted their own search, prosecutors said Jackson fired the weapon, and a roughly five-minute standoff followed involving more than 90 commands and a stun gun before officers and hospital security opened fire, striking him in the head, chest, abdomen, buttocks, and thighs. A Franklin County grand jury declined to indict any of the Columbus police officers or Mount Carmel security personnel involved in October 2022. No one has ever been charged in Jackson's death.

name: Sahleem Tindle
summary: Sahleem Tindle, 28, a father of two, was shot three times in the back and killed by Bay Area Rapid Transit Police Officer Joseph Mateu on January 3, 2018, on a sidewalk across from the West Oakland BART station. Tindle had been walking to the station with his fiancee and children when he got into an altercation with another man, and the two ended up wrestling over a handgun after shots were fired. Mateu, responding on foot to the sound of gunfire, found the two men grappling and shot Tindle three times without having established who fired the earlier shots or possessed the gun. Alameda County District Attorney Nancy O'Malley cleared Mateu of criminal wrongdoing in October 2018, concluding he reasonably believed he was acting in self-defense and defense of others. In March 2020, a federal jury found Mateu used excessive force and was negligent, awarding Tindle's family $6.3 million. No one has ever been criminally charged in Tindle's death.

name: Aaron Bailey
summary: Aaron Bailey, 45, was shot four times in the back and killed by Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Officers Michal Dinnsen and Carlton Howard on June 29, 2017, moments after crashing his car into a tree at the end of a brief nighttime pursuit. Officers said Bailey ignored commands to show his hands and reached into the center console, where they feared a gun might be stored; no weapon was ever found in the car. Officers fired 11 shots into the back and side of the vehicle. A special prosecutor declined to bring criminal charges in October 2017, and federal investigators separately found insufficient evidence for civil rights charges. In a rare turn, IMPD's own police chief concluded the shooting was not justified and recommended both officers be fired — but Indianapolis's Civilian Police Merit Board voted 5-2 in May 2018 to clear them of any policy violation, allowing them to keep their jobs. No one has ever been held criminally or departmentally accountable for Bailey's death.

name: Delrawn Small
summary: Delrawn Small, 37, a father of three, was shot and killed by off-duty NYPD Officer Wayne Isaacs on July 4, 2016, in East New York, Brooklyn, after the two men were involved in a traffic dispute that authorities said continued for several blocks. Small got out of his car and approached Isaacs's vehicle at a stoplight; Isaacs shot him through the driver's-side window, then briefly got out, looked toward Small as he collapsed, and drove away without identifying himself as police or rendering aid. Isaacs testified Small had punched him and that he feared for his life, but surveillance video played at trial appeared to contradict that account, showing Small shot almost immediately upon reaching the car. New York's Attorney General, appointed special prosecutor under a new state policy for police killings of unarmed civilians, charged Isaacs with second-degree murder. A Brooklyn jury acquitted him of all charges in November 2017. No one has ever been convicted in Small's death.

name: Yvette Smith
summary: Yvette Smith, 47, a mother of two who had survived cancer, was shot twice and killed by Bastrop County, Texas Sheriff's Deputy Daniel Willis on February 16, 2014, moments after she opened the front door of her Camp Swift home. Smith had called 911 herself to report her boyfriend and his son fighting over a shotgun; by the time deputies arrived, she had already persuaded them to unload the gun and put it away. A dispatcher nonetheless told Willis someone inside had a gun, and he retrieved an AR-15 from his patrol car. Dashcam video showed no deputy gave any command before Willis fired the moment Smith appeared in the doorway; she was unarmed. Willis was charged with murder and fired from the department. His first trial ended in a hung jury deadlocked 8-4 toward conviction; at his retrial, Willis waived a jury and was acquitted by a judge in April 2016. No one has ever been convicted in Smith's death.

name: Charly “Africa” Keunang
summary: Charly Leundeu Keunang, 43, a Cameroonian national living homeless on Skid Row and known locally as “Africa,” was shot five times and killed by three Los Angeles Police officers on March 1, 2015, during a struggle that began when officers tried to arrest him on suspicion of robbery. A bystander's cellphone video of the daylight shooting was viewed millions of times worldwide and sparked days of protest under the banner “Justice For Africa.” Police said Keunang grabbed a rookie officer's holstered gun during the struggle, but the family's attorney later showed his DNA was never found on the weapon, despite the police chief's initial public claim that it had been. The LAPD Police Commission ruled the shooting justified in 2016, and the Los Angeles County District Attorney declined to bring charges later that year. A federal jury nonetheless found two officers liable in 2018, and the city settled with Keunang's family for $1.95 million. No one has ever been criminally charged in Keunang's death.

name: Robert Lawrence White
summary: Robert Lawrence White, 41, a man with cognitive impairments, was shot and killed by Montgomery County, Maryland Police Officer Anand Badgujar in a Silver Spring parking lot on June 11, 2018. White was simply walking alone near his home when Badgujar, who had just finished an unrelated call, noticed a rip in his jacket and moved his hand toward his pocket, and began following him. The encounter escalated into a physical struggle in which White allegedly knocked the officer down; Badgujar, heard on his own radio describing the situation as a possible “suicide by cop type thing,” fired eight rounds, striking White multiple times. No weapon was found on White. The Howard County State's Attorney's Office, brought in for an independent review, unanimously cleared Badgujar of criminal wrongdoing in July 2018, and Montgomery County's own internal review reached the same conclusion in 2019. A federal lawsuit alleging White was targeted because he was Black was dismissed in 2023. No one has ever been charged in White's death.

name: O'Shae Terry
summary: O'Shae Terry, 24, was shot four times and killed by Arlington, Texas Police Officer Bau Tran on September 1, 2018, during a traffic stop for an expired registration tag. After officers said they smelled marijuana, Terry began rolling up his windows and started the engine to drive away; Tran, who had climbed onto the SUV's running board, drew his weapon and fired five rounds through the window as the vehicle began moving, striking Terry four times. A Tarrant County grand jury indicted Tran on criminally negligent homicide eight months later, a rare criminal charge against a police officer in the county. In May 2023, nearly five years after the shooting, Tran pleaded guilty — but received deferred adjudication, meaning he served no jail time and, if he completes probation, will have no conviction on his record at all. A separate federal civil rights lawsuit was dismissed on qualified immunity grounds. No one has ever been convicted in Terry's death.

name: Vincent Truitt
summary: Vincent Truitt, 17, was shot twice in the back and killed by a Cobb County, Georgia Police officer on July 13, 2020, after fleeing on foot from a car that had been reported stolen. Truitt was the front-seat passenger; after the driver jumped out and was caught, Truitt also ran, and an officer chased him roughly two seconds — with no verbal commands given, according to released video — before firing. Police said Truitt had a gun and pointed it at the officer during the chase, though the officer's own body camera footage of that moment was reportedly too blurry to clearly confirm it. A Cobb County grand jury deliberated roughly eight hours in February 2021 before ruling the shooting justified. The family's $150 million federal lawsuit, which attorneys called the largest ever filed in a Georgia police shooting case, was later dismissed on qualified immunity grounds. No one has ever been charged in Truitt's death.

name: William Green
summary: William Green, 43, was shot six times and killed by Prince George's County, Maryland Police Corporal Michael Owen Jr. while handcuffed in the front seat of Owen's patrol car on January 27, 2020. Owen had found Green asleep in his own vehicle after a series of traffic crashes, apparently under the influence of an unknown substance, handcuffed him, and placed him in the cruiser's passenger seat. Owen, who was not wearing a body camera, testified Green body-slammed him and grabbed for his gun during a struggle inside the car; prosecutors argued there was no evidence Green ever touched the weapon. Owen was fired and charged with second-degree murder within days, becoming the first officer in county history charged with murder for an on-duty killing. After nearly four years of delay, a jury acquitted him of all four charges in December 2023 following roughly two hours of deliberation. No one has ever been convicted in Green's death.

name: Anthony Lowe Jr.
summary: Anthony Lowe Jr., 36, a double amputee who used a wheelchair, was shot roughly 10 times and killed by two Huntington Park, California police officers on January 26, 2023, moments after he moved away from his wheelchair while holding a knife. Officers had responded to a report that Lowe stabbed a man in the chest; police said he ignored commands to drop the knife and threatened to throw it after Tasers failed to stop him. Cellphone video showed him on the sidewalk moving away from the wheelchair as officers approached. Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman's office announced in December 2025, nearly three years after the shooting, that it would not file charges, concluding in a 28-page report that Lowe “despite his physical limitations, presented an imminent deadly threat.” No one has ever been charged in Lowe's death.

name: Christopher DeAndre Mitchell
summary: Christopher DeAndre Mitchell, 23, was shot and killed by Torrance, California Police Officers Matthew Concannon and Anthony Chavez on December 9, 2018, within seconds of them approaching a parked car matching a stolen-vehicle report. Officers said they saw Mitchell reach toward what turned out to be an altered air rifle wedged between his legs and that he failed to comply with commands; his family maintained he was asleep and never given a chance to surrender. Then-District Attorney Jackie Lacey's office declined to file charges in 2019, finding the shooting justified. After George Gascón took office pledging to revisit police shootings, his office reopened the case in 2023 and secured a grand jury indictment for voluntary manslaughter — the same year it was publicly revealed that both officers had exchanged racist text messages. In November 2025, under a new district attorney, prosecutors moved to dismiss the case, and a judge granted that dismissal in April 2026, citing insufficient evidence to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. No one has ever been convicted in Mitchell's death.

name: Jor'Dell Richardson
summary: Jor'Dell Richardson, 14, was shot and killed by Aurora, Colorado Police Officer Roch Gruszeczka on June 1, 2023, seconds after being tackled at the end of a foot chase following a suspected robbery of a convenience store. Body camera video showed Richardson reaching toward his waistband as officers chased him into an alley; Officer James Snapp tackled him, and five seconds later Gruszeczka fired a single shot into his upper abdomen while shouting “Gun, gun. Let go of the [expletive] gun.” The weapon turned out to be a pellet-gun replica of a 9mm pistol. Richardson pleaded for help and lost consciousness within moments; he was pronounced dead at a hospital. The 18th Judicial District Attorney's Office announced in September 2023, three months later, that Gruszeczka was legally justified and would face no charges. No one has ever been charged in Richardson's death.

name: Omari Cryer
summary: Omari Cryer, 25, a father, was shot twice and killed by a deputy U.S. Marshal on May 20, 2022, in Louisville's Chickasaw neighborhood while a federal task force attempted to serve a domestic violence arrest warrant. Body camera video showed Cryer running from officers, hopping a fence, and pulling a handgun from his waistband before falling; a marshal fired two rounds, striking him in the front. No other officer discharged a weapon. Nearly a year later, Cryer's family said the Jefferson County Commonwealth's Attorney's Office told them it did not have enough evidence to indict anyone in his death. In 2023, a complaint to Louisville's Office of Inspector General alleged the arrest warrant used to justify the operation itself contained false statements; LMPD's chief publicly denied that allegation. No one has ever been charged in Cryer's death, and the identity of the marshal who fired has never been publicly released.

name: Linus Phillip
summary: Linus F. Phillip, 30, was shot four times and killed by Largo, Florida Police Officer Matthew Steiner at a Wawa gas station on March 23, 2018, after a traffic stop for illegally tinted windows. Officers said they smelled marijuana and moved to detain Phillip; he got back into his car and reversed, with Steiner partly inside the vehicle. Police said Steiner, being dragged and pinned between the car and gas pumps, fired in self-defense. Investigators later acknowledged that surveillance footage from the gas station did not actually capture the shooting itself. Weeks later, Largo detectives traveled to the funeral home holding Phillip's body and pressed his finger to his phone in an attempt to unlock it, a move his family called a violation. The State Attorney's Office ruled the shooting justifiable homicide in April 2018. No one has ever been charged in Phillip's death.

name: Kenneth Ross Jr.
summary: Kenneth Ross Jr., 25, was shot in the back and shoulder and killed by Gardena, California Police Officer Michael Robbins with a rifle on April 11, 2018, as Ross ran away from officers responding to a report of a man firing a weapon in Rowley Memorial Park. Body and dash camera video reviewed by the family's attorney showed Ross running with his hands empty and his back to police when Robbins fired two shots from an AR-15. Robbins told investigators he believed Ross was reaching for a gun and feared for his life; a handgun was later recovered from Ross's shorts, which his family disputes he was carrying at the moment he was shot. The Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office cleared Robbins of criminal wrongdoing in June 2019, finding he acted in lawful self-defense. Robbins had been involved in three prior shootings before this one and retired from the department in 2020. No one has ever been charged in Ross's death.

name: DeCynthia Clements
summary: DeCynthia Clements, 34, was shot three times and killed by Elgin, Illinois Police Lieutenant Christian Jensen on Interstate 90 on March 12, 2018, at the end of an hour-long roadside standoff during which she appeared to be in mental distress and set her own car on fire. As smoke filled the vehicle, she opened the door and stepped out; police said she was holding a knife, though it is not clearly visible in released video. Jensen fired despite other officers on scene being equipped with a stun gun and rubber-bullet-firing weapon, telling investigators he could not wait to see if less-lethal options would work given how close officers were standing. A medical examiner found cocaine in her system. The Cook County State's Attorney's Office declined to file charges in February 2019, a decision a separate state appellate prosecutor's review upheld. No one has ever been charged in Clements's death.

name: Joshua Ruffin
summary: Joshua “Josh” Dariandre Ruffin, 17, was shot and killed by Columbia, South Carolina Police Officer Kevin Davis on April 8, 2020, after Davis noticed him during a patrol responding to reports of car break-ins and neighborhood suspicious activity during COVID-19 lockdown hours. Ruffin ran when Davis tried to stop him; during the roughly 30-second, 557-foot chase, Davis said Ruffin stopped, pulled a .45-caliber handgun from a bag, and pointed it at him, prompting Davis to fire 10 shots, one striking Ruffin in the forehead. Fifth Circuit Solicitor Byron Gipson, who is also Black, announced in June 2020 that Davis would not be charged, openly acknowledging “a racial dynamic” to the case before concluding it played no role in his decision. The Ruffin family's attorney said the released body camera footage was too blurry to actually confirm Ruffin pointed the gun at Davis. No one has ever been charged in Ruffin's death.

name: Jeremy McDole
summary: Jeremy “Bam Bam” McDole, 28, a paraplegic who used a wheelchair, was shot and killed by four Wilmington, Delaware police officers on September 23, 2015, after a 911 caller falsely reported he had a gun and had shot himself; the caller later recanted the claim and was never penalized for it. Bystander cellphone video showed officers surrounding McDole in his wheelchair, repeatedly ordering him to drop a weapon and raise his hands, before Officer Joseph Dellose opened fire as McDole's hands moved near his waist; no gun was ever visible in any released footage, and evidence photos purporting to show the recovered weapon did not surface publicly until six years later. Delaware's Department of Justice cleared all four officers of criminal wrongdoing in 2016, while finding Dellose's conduct “extraordinarily poor”; a 2020 review reached the identical conclusion. No one has ever been charged in McDole's death.

name: Trey Pringle
summary: Trey Pringle, 24, a man with a documented history of mental illness, died three days after Beaufort County, South Carolina sheriff's deputies Tased him multiple times during a welfare check at his family's home on February 17, 2018. His family called 911 specifically requesting medical assistance. The situation escalated inside the home; deputies said Pringle struck and kicked them before he was Tased repeatedly and restrained, and a firefighter assisting on scene, Brandon Corey Thomsen, was separately accused in a wrongful death lawsuit of placing Pringle in a chokehold. Pringle suffered cardiac arrest and was taken to Beaufort Memorial Hospital, where he died three days later. Medical examiners at the Medical University of South Carolina ruled the death a homicide. After an eight-month investigation, 14th Circuit Solicitor Duffie Stone announced in February 2019 that no criminal charges would be filed against anyone involved. No one has ever been charged in Pringle's death.

name: Deandre Brunston
summary: Deandre “Trey” Brunston, 24, was shot 22 times and killed after Los Angeles County Sheriff's deputies fired 81 rounds at him in a doorway in Compton on August 24, 2003, following a 30-minute standoff after his girlfriend called police over a domestic dispute. Brunston falsely claimed to be armed and wanted for murder in an apparent effort to avoid returning to prison on a probation violation; deputies released a K-9 unit toward him despite the on-scene K-9 handler having judged the situation “non-deployable” and objecting to the order, which was given by a supervising lieutenant later found to have been drinking at a party when he issued it. Brunston dropped the object in his hand — a sandal, not a weapon — as the dog reached him, but deputies had already begun firing. No gun was ever found on or near him. No criminal charges were ever filed against any deputy. The wounded police dog was airlifted to a veterinary hospital while Brunston was left on the concrete steps.

name: Omar Edwards
summary: Omar Edwards, 25, an off-duty NYPD officer, was shot and killed by a fellow officer, Sergeant Andrew Dunton, in East Harlem on May 28, 2009, moments after Edwards had chased a man who broke into his personal car. Edwards, in plainclothes with his badge not visible, ran toward Dunton's unmarked car with his own service weapon drawn while pursuing the suspect; Dunton, believing Edwards was a threat, fired six times, striking him in the arm, hip, and back. No witness reported hearing Edwards identify himself as a police officer before the shooting, and he never fired his own weapon. A Manhattan grand jury, after hearing from 20 witnesses and reviewing 68 documents, declined to indict Dunton in September 2009. Civil rights leaders questioned whether the outcome would have been different had the officers' races been reversed. No one has ever been criminally charged in Edwards's death.

name: Roger Malcom, Dorothy Malcom, George Dorsey & Mae Murray Dorsey
summary: Roger Malcom, 24, his wife Dorothy Malcom, 20, and another sharecropper couple, World War II veteran George Dorsey, 28, and his wife Mae Murray Dorsey, 24, were shot and killed by a mob of 20 to 25 white men at Moore's Ford Bridge near Monroe, Georgia on July 25, 1946, in what became known as “the last mass lynching in America.” Roger Malcom had stabbed a white farmer, Barnett Hester, in a dispute eleven days earlier and was released on bond that afternoon; their employer, Loy Harrison, was driving the two couples home when the car was stopped at the bridge by an armed mob who dragged all four out, tied them up, and shot them so many times the bodies were difficult to identify. The killings prompted President Harry Truman to push for federal civil rights legislation and create the President's Committee on Civil Rights, but a 1946 federal grand jury failed to indict anyone, concluding only that the four died “at the hands of persons unknown.” Despite renewed state and federal investigations in 2001 and 2008 that recovered Ku Klux Klan membership records and firearms from a suspect's property, the FBI and Georgia Bureau of Investigation formally closed the case on January 29, 2018 — 72 years later — without ever charging anyone.

name: Winston Boogie Smith Jr.
summary: Winston “Boogie” Smith Jr., 32, a father of three and local comedian, was shot and killed by members of a U.S. Marshals Service fugitive task force in an Uptown Minneapolis parking ramp on June 3, 2021, while sitting in an SUV with a woman he had been on a lunch date with. Task force members had watched the couple for over an hour before boxing in Smith's vehicle and announcing an arrest on an outstanding firearms warrant; officials said he refused to comply and produced a handgun, and task force members fired. No body camera, dashcam, or surveillance footage of the shooting exists — the Marshals Service had not yet implemented a body camera policy change in Minnesota specifically, despite the change taking effect elsewhere months earlier. His companion's attorneys said she never saw Smith holding a gun, and investigators never took gunshot residue samples from his hands because his body had already been washed by the medical examiner. Crow Wing County Attorney Donald Ryan declined to charge any task force member in October 2021. No one has ever been charged in Smith's death.

name: Frederick Cox Jr.
summary: Frederick Rodriquez Smith Cox Jr., 18, was shot and killed by a plainclothes Davidson County, North Carolina sheriff's detective outside a funeral at Living Water Baptist Church in High Point on November 8, 2020, after gunfire broke out in the parking lot as mourners were leaving. Witnesses said Cox was helping people get to safety when Detective Michael Shane Hill, who was attending the funeral of a separate homicide victim he had been investigating, shot him multiple times. Hill said he saw Cox holding a handgun, and a gun was found near his body afterward, but Cox's autopsy found no gunshot residue on his hands, meaning he had not fired a weapon. The state medical examiner ruled his death a homicide. A Guilford County grand jury declined to indict Hill in June 2021, seven months after the shooting. No one has ever been charged in Cox's death.

name: Najee Seabrooks
summary: Najee Seabrooks, 31, a violence-intervention specialist with the Paterson Healing Collective, was shot and killed by two Paterson, New Jersey police officers on March 3, 2023, at the end of a roughly five-hour standoff after he called 911 himself during a mental health crisis, saying people were trying to hurt him. He barricaded himself in a bathroom with knives; officers fired 15 non-lethal rounds without effect as he cut himself and set a fire, before he emerged and, according to the Attorney General's office, lunged at officers with a knife. Of roughly 220 minutes of body camera footage from seven officers later released, the knife was clearly visible in only one recording; most captured the shooting itself without a clear view of a weapon in his hand. A state grand jury declined to indict either officer in March 2025, two years after the shooting. No one has ever been charged in Seabrooks's death.

name: Da'Quain Johnson
summary: Da'Quain Johnson, 32, a father of three daughters, was shot three times and killed by a Grand Rapids, Michigan Police Department K-9 officer on February 18, 2026, in an apartment complex parking lot after being chased on his bicycle and attacked by a police dog. Officers said they believed Johnson, who was on parole for a prior weapons conviction, was armed, and that he pointed a gun at an officer during the struggle after falling from his bike; a handgun was recovered near his body. A video released by Johnson's family appeared to show him lying face-down, pinned by an officer and still being bitten by the K-9, in the moments before he was shot. Kent County Prosecutor Chris Becker announced on April 2, 2026 that neither officer would be charged, holding the news conference at a Michigan State Police facility roughly seven miles from his own downtown office rather than there. No one has ever been charged in Johnson's death.

name: Jalen Randle
summary: Jalen Randle, 29, was shot in the neck and killed by Houston Police Officer Shane Privette on April 27, 2022, roughly two seconds after stepping out of a car at the end of a short chase in the Pleasantville neighborhood. Officers had been trying to serve Randle with a warrant on three felony charges. Body camera video showed Privette order Randle to show his hands and open fire before finishing the sentence, then curse after the shot; Randle dropped a bag that was later found to contain a gun. Harris County presented the case to a grand jury twice — the first took no action at all in April 2023, and a second panel declined to indict Privette in October 2023, 18 months after the shooting. Privette was later returned to active duty in the department's narcotics division. No one has ever been charged in Randle's death.

name: Luke Stewart
summary: Luke Stewart, 23, was shot and killed by Euclid, Ohio Police Officer Matthew Rhodes in the early morning hours of March 13, 2017, after officers found him asleep in a parked car reported as suspicious. Neither Rhodes nor his partner, Officer Louis Catalani, identified themselves as police before approaching the vehicle, both later testified; when Stewart woke and started driving away, Rhodes climbed partway into the moving car, deployed a Taser and struck Stewart repeatedly, then shot him as the car struck the patrol vehicle. Stewart was unarmed. A grand jury declined to indict Rhodes later that year. Neither officer wore a body camera. A federal judge dismissed the family's civil rights lawsuit, a decision upheld on appeal and left standing when the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear the case in 2021 — yet a Cuyahoga County jury, hearing a separate state wrongful-death claim in November 2022, awarded Stewart's family $4.4 million, finding Rhodes had acted recklessly. No one has ever been criminally charged in Stewart's death.

name: Ricky Cobb II
summary: Ricky Cobb II, 33, was shot twice and killed by Minnesota State Trooper Ryan Londregan on Interstate 94 in Minneapolis on July 31, 2023, during a traffic stop for a taillight violation. Troopers learned Cobb was wanted in a separate county for violating a domestic no-contact order and ordered him out of the car; when he refused and began driving away while a trooper was partly inside attempting to unbuckle his seatbelt, Londregan fired twice into his torso. Londregan was charged in January 2024 with second-degree murder, first-degree assault, and manslaughter, becoming a rare instance of a Minnesota trooper facing criminal charges. Five months later, the Hennepin County Attorney dropped every charge before trial, citing new evidence that Londregan would testify Cobb reached for his firearm and that state training did not, contrary to best practice, instruct troopers against shooting into a moving vehicle. A federal judge separately dismissed the family's civil lawsuit. No one has ever been convicted in Cobb's death.

name: Thomas Shipp & Abram Smith
summary: Thomas Shipp and Abram Smith were lynched by a mob of thousands in the town square of Marion, Indiana, on the night of August 7, 1930, after being arrested the previous evening in connection with the death of a white factory worker, Claude Deeter, and an alleged assault on his companion, Mary Ball. The mob broke into the county jail with sledgehammers and crowbars, dragged both men from their cells, beat them, and hanged them from a tree as thousands of local residents, including women and children, looked on and posed for photographs. A third young man held in connection with the same incident, 16-year-old James Cameron, had a noose already around his neck when the mob inexplicably released him. Local photographer Lawrence Beitler's image of the hanging became the most widely reproduced lynching photograph in American history and directly inspired the poem and song “Strange Fruit,” later made famous by Billie Holiday. No one was ever charged in connection with the lynching of Shipp or Smith.

name: David Jones
summary: David Jones, 30, was shot twice in the back and killed by Philadelphia Police Officer Ryan Pownall on June 8, 2017, after being pulled over for riding a dirt bike illegally on a city street. Officers said Pownall found a gun on Jones during a pat-down and struggled with him over the weapon before it fell and Jones fled on foot; Pownall then fired multiple shots, striking Jones twice in the back. He was the first Philadelphia officer in roughly two decades to be charged with murder for an on-duty shooting. After more than five years of pretrial proceedings, including an appeal that reached the Pennsylvania Supreme Court over how juries should be instructed on police use-of-force law, a Philadelphia judge dismissed all charges against Pownall in October 2022, ruling prosecutors had improperly instructed the grand jury that indicted him. Pownall was reinstated to the police department with full back pay and seniority in 2024. No one has ever been convicted in Jones's death.

name: Kemonte Cobbs
summary: Kemonte Cobbs, 15, was shot and killed by Gary, Indiana Police Officer Justin Hedrick during a foot pursuit on August 1, 2017, after Cobbs and several other teenagers were reportedly involved in an attempted armed robbery in neighboring Munster. Officers gave shifting and inconsistent accounts of the shooting, variously describing Cobbs as running when shot, lying in wait to ambush pursuing officers, or charging at them with a gun drawn. His mother, Tasheena Brooks, said investigators initially told her no weapon had been recovered at the scene, then called a week later to say one had been found near his body. Lake County Prosecutor Bernard Carter ruled the shooting justified and declined to file charges. Community members held sustained protests demanding the release of video and audio recordings, which authorities resisted for months. No one has ever been charged in Cobbs's death.

name: Darryl Tyree Williams
summary: Darryl “Tyree” Williams, 32, died in Raleigh, North Carolina police custody on January 17, 2023, after officers on a “proactive patrol” approached him sitting in his parked car outside a sweepstakes parlor and, suspecting drug possession, tried to arrest him. Williams ran, fell, and was tased repeatedly — by some accounts three to four times — while telling officers he had a heart condition, audible on the body camera footage later released. He went into cardiac arrest and died at the hospital. The state medical examiner ruled his death a homicide, attributing it to sudden cardiac arrest amid cocaine intoxication, physical exertion, Taser use, and physical restraint together. Wake County District Attorney Lorrin Freeman announced in June 2023 that the officers' actions did not violate the law and that prosecution was “unsustainable.” The City of Raleigh settled a federal civil rights lawsuit with Williams's family for $975,000 in December 2025. No one has ever been charged in Williams's death.

name: James Lanier
summary: James Lanier, 34, who had a history of mental illness, was shot and killed by a Wallace, North Carolina police officer outside the Express Mini Mart on February 24, 2023, after store employees called police because he had entered the store naked and was bothering customers. According to the district attorney's account of surveillance video, Lanier pushed the responding officer, was Tased without apparent effect, and continued advancing on the officer despite repeated commands to back away before the officer fired three shots, one of which struck and killed him. District Attorney Ernie Lee ruled the shooting justified in May 2023, and later cited toxicology results showing PCP in Lanier's system as further justification. Lanier's father publicly said he believed race played a role in his son's death. No one has ever been charged in Lanier's death.

name: Mary Turner & Hayes Turner
summary: Mary Turner, 19 and eight months pregnant, and her husband Hayes Turner, 25, were lynched one day apart in Brooks County, Georgia, in May 1918, during a mob rampage that killed at least 11 to 13 Black people in the wake of a white plantation owner's murder. After Hampton Smith, known locally for abusing Black farmworkers, was shot and killed by an employee named Sidney Johnson on May 16, 1918, a mob of hundreds began seizing and lynching Black residents with no connection to any investigation, based only on rumor. Hayes Turner, who had previously been jailed for threatening Smith after Smith beat Mary, was seized from sheriff's custody and lynched on May 18. When Mary Turner publicly denounced her husband's killing and vowed to seek warrants against the men responsible, a mob of several hundred captured her the next day, hanged her upside down from a tree, and burned and shot her to death; she was still alive when a member of the mob cut her unborn child from her body. No one was ever charged in the deaths of Mary Turner, Hayes Turner, or the other Black residents killed during the same two-week rampage.

name: Allen Brooks
summary: Allen Brooks, roughly 59 years old and possibly born into slavery, was lynched by a mob estimated at 2,000 to 6,000 people in downtown Dallas, Texas, on March 3, 1910, on the day he was set to stand trial. Brooks, a handyman, had been accused of assaulting a two-and-a-half-year-old white girl whose family's furnace he had been repairing; the director of a Dallas civil rights organization later told The New York Times there was no proof he was guilty. As his trial recessed at the Dallas County Courthouse, a mob of over 1,000 people overwhelmed 70 to 150 law enforcement officers, tied a rope around Brooks's neck, and pulled him out a second-story window; he landed on his head on the street below, was beaten further by the crowd, and was dragged by car to a nearby arch where he was hanged from a telephone pole or iron spike. Souvenir postcards of the lynching were printed and mailed by the thousands. No one was ever charged in Brooks's death, and the site went unmarked for 111 years.

name: Dexter Reed
summary: Dexter Reed, 26, was shot 13 times and killed by Chicago police officers on March 21, 2024, during a traffic stop in the city's Humboldt Park neighborhood that escalated into a gunfight. Five plainclothes tactical officers in an unmarked SUV curbed Reed's car, giving shifting reasons for the stop — first a seatbelt violation, later tinted windows. Officers said Reed, who did not legally own the recovered handgun, fired first and wounded one officer, prompting four others to fire a combined 96 rounds in 41 seconds. Chicago's Civilian Office of Police Accountability separately found the same five officers had conducted roughly 50 traffic stops in the days beforehand, including two documented instances of unlawfully stopping and detaining people without justification. Cook County State's Attorney Eileen O'Neill Burke announced in August 2025, nearly a year and a half after the shooting, that none of the officers would be charged. No one has ever been charged in Reed's death.

name: Bunk Richardson
summary: Bunk Richardson was abducted from the Etowah County Jail in Gadsden, Alabama, by a large white mob in the middle of the night on February 11, 1906, and lynched, despite never having been charged with any crime. In July 1905, three men had been accused of raping and murdering a white woman; Richardson was not involved but was arrested anyway because he knew one of the suspects. Two of the actual suspects were later tried, convicted, and executed; the third, Will Johnson, was also convicted and sentenced to death, but Alabama Governor William Jelks, doubting his guilt, commuted the sentence to life in prison. That commutation of a stranger's sentence sparked outrage in Gadsden, and a mob responded by seizing Richardson — who had no connection to the original crime beyond an acquaintance — dragging him through the streets, and hanging him from train trestles over the Coosa River. His relatives were forced to flee town and abandon their businesses. No one was ever charged in Richardson's death, and the site went without any public acknowledgment for 110 years until a historical marker was dedicated in 2016.

name: The Colfax Massacre
summary: On Easter Sunday, April 13, 1873, a mob of armed white men, including former Confederate soldiers and Ku Klux Klan members, attacked the Grant Parish Courthouse in Colfax, Louisiana, where Black freedmen and state militia had gathered to defend the results of a disputed election. The mob, numbering as many as 150 to 300 and equipped with a small cannon, set the courthouse ablaze; most of the Black men inside were shot as they fled the flames or after they had already surrendered, and nearly 50 more were murdered later that night after being held as prisoners for hours. Estimates of the death toll vary significantly across sources, ranging from roughly 62 to as many as 150 or more Black men killed; only three of the white attackers died. Federal prosecutors indicted 97 people and brought nine to trial; a jury convicted three men under the Enforcement Act of 1870, but the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously overturned every conviction in United States v. Cruikshank (1876), ruling the federal government lacked power to prosecute private individuals for violating civil rights. No one was ever held accountable for what remains the deadliest single incident of racial violence during Reconstruction.

name: Frank Tyson
summary: Frank Tyson, 53, died in the custody of Canton, Ohio police officers Camden Burch and Beau Schoenegge on April 18, 2024, after they restrained him face-down on the floor of a veterans hall he had entered following a car crash. Body camera video showed Tyson repeatedly telling officers “They're trying to kill me” and, after being handcuffed with an officer's knee on his upper body, “I can't breathe”; an officer told him “You're fine. Shut the [expletive] up.” Tyson was left motionless and unattended for roughly seven minutes before officers checked on him. The Stark County coroner ruled his death a homicide. A grand jury indicted both officers on felony reckless homicide charges in November 2024, making Tyson's case one of the rare instances to reach that point. Nearly two years later, on the day jury selection began for their trial, both officers instead pleaded guilty to unrelated misdemeanor charges — failure to report a crime and dereliction of duty — neither of which addresses causing Tyson's death, and the original reckless homicide charges were dropped. No one has ever been convicted of causing Tyson's death.

name: Roshad McIntosh
summary: Roshad McIntosh, 19, was shot and killed by Chicago Police Officer Robert Slechter on August 24, 2014, after being chased into the yard of a residence in the North Lawndale neighborhood. Police said McIntosh pointed a gun at Slechter, who fired three shots; a loaded pistol was recovered at the scene, though no usable fingerprints were ever identified on it. Witnesses told McIntosh's family he was actually kneeling on the ground with his hands raised, unarmed, when he was shot, and his family's attorneys have alleged the gun was planted after the fact. Chicago's Independent Police Review Authority cleared Slechter in 2015; after the agency was replaced by the Civilian Office of Police Accountability, the case was reopened at the family's request and, after a two-year investigation, COPA again found the shooting justified. A separate officer at the scene was recommended for firing after his account was contradicted by surveillance footage, but he retired before the Police Board acted. The City of Chicago moved to settle the family's federal lawsuit for $2.25 million a decade after the shooting. No one has ever been charged in McIntosh's death.

name: Kevin Peterson Jr.
summary: Kevin Peterson Jr., 21, a new father, was shot 34 times and killed by three Clark County, Washington Sheriff's deputies on October 29, 2020, after he ran from a drug sting in a bank parking lot near Vancouver. Clark County's sheriff publicly stated the day after the shooting that Peterson had fired at deputies; an independent multi-agency investigation concluded roughly two weeks later that he never fired his weapon at all, though he had one on him. Surveillance video showed Peterson was shot from behind while running away. His body was left in the parking lot for roughly eleven hours before being removed. An independent prosecutor from a neighboring county found the shooting justified in August 2021, concluding Peterson had “ample opportunity” to drop his gun and declining to charge any of the three deputies. The family's federal wrongful death lawsuit settled for $1.25 million in late 2024. No one has ever been charged in Peterson's death.

name: Damian Daniels
summary: Damian Daniels, 30, a Black Army combat veteran who had served in Afghanistan, was shot and killed by Bexar County, Texas Sheriff's Deputy John Rodriguez outside his home on August 25, 2020, during a mental health welfare check requested by his family. Deputies, including Sheriff Javier Salazar himself, responded and said Daniels became erratic and reached for a legally owned gun in his waistband, leading to a physical struggle that lasted more than two minutes before Rodriguez opened fire, striking him twice. Sheriff Salazar's early public account, including selectively released still images, drew accusations from the family of “material misrepresentations” before full body camera footage was ever made public. A Bexar County grand jury declined to indict Rodriguez in December 2021, roughly 16 months after the shooting. No one has ever been charged in Daniels's death.

name: Donnie Sanders
summary: Donnie Sanders, 47, was shot three times and killed by Kansas City, Missouri Police Officer Blayne Newton on March 12, 2020, after a foot chase that began with what prosecutors later called a “pretextual” traffic stop — Newton had no radar equipment or training to legally have clocked Sanders for speeding in the first place. Sanders fled on foot into an alley; Newton fired five shots, striking him three times. Police initially said Sanders was unarmed, carrying only a cellphone. Jackson County Prosecutor Jean Peters Baker declined to charge Newton in March 2021, citing a witness who said Sanders appeared to be pointing something at the officer. Newton remained on the force and, within the following years, accumulated multiple excessive force allegations — including kneeling on a nine-months-pregnant woman's back during an arrest — before fatally shooting two more people in a single 2026 encounter. Prosecutor Baker then publicly called for Newton's firing, citing “years of institutional failure to act.” No one has ever been charged in Sanders's death.

name: Tyrea Pryor
summary: Tyrea Pryor Sr., 39, a father of three, was shot approximately 15 times and killed by Independence, Missouri Police Officers Hunter Soule and Jamie Welsh on March 11, 2022, after a police pursuit ended in a crash. Pryor was left incapacitated and trapped in the wrecked vehicle; an assault-style rifle was found lodged in the car but never brandished, and another officer had already secured it before Soule and Welsh opened fire, believing Pryor was reaching for a pistol. No pistol was ever found — investigators later theorized a pill bottle in his waistband may have been mistaken for one. Jackson County Prosecutor Jean Peters Baker announced in March 2023, a year after the shooting, that she would not charge either officer, stating it was “indisputable Pryor did not have a gun in his hand” but that officers held a “reasonable belief” a threat existed. Pryor's family filed a $25 million federal lawsuit and formally asked the Department of Justice to investigate after Baker declined to bring the case before a grand jury. No one has ever been charged in Pryor's death.

name: Xzavier Hill
summary: Xzavier Deyonte Hill, 18, of Charlottesville, was shot and killed by Virginia State Police Troopers Benjamin Bone and Seth Layton on Interstate 64 in Goochland County on January 9, 2021, after a high-speed chase ended when his car slid down an embankment. Troopers said Hill reached for and displayed a handgun as they ordered him to show his hands; dashcam audio captured them shouting “Gun! Gun! Gun!” before firing. A stolen handgun was recovered in the passenger seat after the shooting. A multi-jurisdictional grand jury, overseen by a prosecutor who was himself a former state trooper, unanimously found the shooting justified in February 2021. Hill's mother, Latoya Benton, disputed the official account, said her son did not have a gun, and accused police of a cover-up; she later filed a $60 million wrongful death lawsuit, and a judge ordered the troopers to answer her questions under oath in the civil case. No one has ever been charged in Hill's death.

name: Jaheim McMillan
summary: Jaheim McMillan, 15, a Gulfport High School freshman, was shot eight times, including once in the head, by Gulfport, Mississippi Police Officer Kenneth Nassar outside a Family Dollar store on October 6, 2022, after officers responded to reports of teenagers waving guns at passing motorists. Police said McMillan fled, then turned toward Nassar with a weapon, prompting the officer to fire; McMillan was taken off life support two days later. A bystander video that circulated afterward appeared to show him already stopped and raising his hands before the shots were fired, directly contradicting the official account. A Harrison County grand jury found “no criminal conduct” on Nassar's part in February 2023, four months after the shooting. His family and civil rights organizers have since formally asked the U.S. Department of Justice's Civil Rights Division to investigate the case. No one has ever been charged in McMillan's death.

name: Paul O'Neal
summary: Paul O'Neal, 18, was shot in the back and killed by Chicago Police Officer Jose Diaz on July 28, 2016, after fleeing on foot from a stolen Jaguar convertible he had crashed into two police vehicles during a chase in the South Shore neighborhood. O'Neal was unarmed. Two other officers had already fired roughly a dozen shots into the car itself before he ran, in apparent violation of the department's own policy against shooting into a moving vehicle when it poses the only danger. The medical examiner classified O'Neal's death a homicide. Following an investigation, no criminal charges were ever filed against any of the three officers who fired. In 2020, the Chicago Police Board fired two of the officers who had shot at the car — but not Diaz, the officer whose shot actually killed O'Neal. The city settled a wrongful death lawsuit with O'Neal's mother for $2.25 million later that year. No one has ever been charged in O'Neal's death.

name: Patrick Warren Sr.
summary: Patrick Lynn Warren Sr., 52, was shot and killed by Killeen, Texas Police Officer Reynaldo Contreras on January 10, 2021, after officers responded to a 911 call specifically requesting a mental health check. Contreras first deployed his Taser, which had no effect on Warren, who was described as emotionally distressed and yelling in his own front yard; when Warren continued to advance, Contreras drew his firearm and fired. Body camera video released by the family's attorney, civil rights lawyer Lee Merritt, captured a bystander repeatedly saying, “I told you, don't use a gun.” Warren's family disputed the department's account, alleging Contreras briefly redirected his weapon toward Warren's wife before returning it to Warren and continuing to fire. A Bell County grand jury declined to indict Contreras in May 2021, four months after the shooting. No one has ever been charged in Warren's death.
